Request

Please prepare a practical Monday-to-Friday watering rota for the Alder Lane learning greenhouse, using the reference notes below. Show who is responsible, the relevant zone, and the suggested time for each task. Account for the stated access arrangements and watering conditions, and make any conditional steps clear. If the notes do not settle a detail needed for the rota, flag it rather than assuming an answer. Keep the rota usable by the volunteers who open the greenhouse.

Reference notes

Alder Lane’s learning greenhouse is a long, narrow structure behind the community center, with its entrance on the south side and a water tap just inside the door. The spring rota covers the second full week of April, when the children’s gardening group meets on Wednesday afternoon and the volunteer team usually works from 8:00 to 10:00 on weekdays. The greenhouse is open to volunteers from 7:30 each morning; the caretaker locks the entrance at 5:30 p.m. No volunteer has a key to the outside hose store, so the rota should rely on the indoor tap and the two blue watering cans already kept beside it. A small hose is available for the central bed, but it must be drained and hung on its hook after use.

The growing areas are divided into four named zones. West Bench holds seed trays and recently pricked-out lettuce and calendula seedlings. The Central Bed contains six tomato plants and a short row of young cucumbers. East Bench is used for herbs, including mature rosemary, mint in separate pots, and newly sown coriander. The Propagation Shelf is a warm, shaded rack with cuttings and two covered trays; its cover is opened during the day and replaced before the greenhouse is locked. Three citrus tubs sit on the floor beside the east wall and are not included in the bench labels. A laminated map showing the four zones and the citrus tubs is clipped to the greenhouse door.

Watering needs differ across the space. The West Bench trays dry faster than the larger pots, but the seedlings should be checked before water is added because the lower trays can remain damp after a cloudy day. The tomato and cucumber bed is watered at soil level, not over the leaves. The rosemary prefers a lighter check than the mint, whose pots are allowed to drain fully into saucers that are emptied after watering. Coriander was sown on Friday and should be kept evenly moist while it germinates. The covered propagation trays are checked each morning for condensation; if the compost is moist and droplets are visible on the inside of the lids, they do not need extra water that day.

Mara Venn coordinates the weekday rota and normally arrives shortly before 8:00. Ivo Park is available Monday, Wednesday, and Friday mornings, while Linh Adebayo can come Tuesday and Thursday before 9:00. Jo Bell leads the children’s group on Wednesday and can supervise a short greenhouse check after 3:15 p.m., but cannot open the building in the morning. Tomas Reed can help on Monday and Thursday and is the only person on the team who has used the small hose; he has asked to be paired with someone for any hose task. Mara said, “If I’m checking the seedlings, I can also note which trays were already damp.” Linh replied, “Please leave the mint saucers empty when you finish; standing water brings fungus gnats.”

The caretaker’s wall thermometer is read at the start of the day and records the overnight minimum as well as the current temperature. The forecast for this week is changeable: Monday is expected to be bright, Tuesday may stay overcast, Wednesday is forecast to be cool, and showers are possible on Thursday. No reliable forecast is posted for Friday. Mara has asked volunteers to use the thermometer and the visible condition of the compost rather than treating the forecast as a watering instruction. If the overnight minimum is below 8°C, delay watering the Central Bed until the greenhouse has warmed, then check the soil again; do not water it early simply to keep to a clock time. This condition applies later in the week too, not just on the morning it is first mentioned.

1. On Monday, Tomas checked the hose connection and found no leak. He watered the central bed at soil level while Mara watched, drained the hose, and returned it to its hook. The West Bench trays were inspected, and two small lettuce trays were watered while the remaining trays were left alone because their compost was still damp. Mara recorded that the trays nearest the door dried first after a sunny weekend. The Propagation Shelf lids had light condensation, so no water was added there. The citrus tubs were checked by lifting the pots slightly; one felt lighter than the others, but the notes do not say whether it was watered.
2. On Tuesday, Linh arrived at 8:10 and found the greenhouse cool and cloudy. She checked the rosemary and mint pots separately, watered the mint, and emptied the saucers before leaving. She wrote that the rosemary compost was still cool and damp. The coriander surface had begun to dry in one corner, so Linh used a small amount of water over that patch. The propagation lids had no visible droplets, and the compost below them felt moist. She left a note asking the next volunteer to check the citrus tubs individually rather than giving all three the same amount.
3. On Wednesday, Ivo is expected before the children’s group, and Jo can make the later supervised check after 3:15. The group will look at the tomato flowers but is not scheduled to water the plants. Jo has a small jug for demonstrations and can return it to the shelf after use. If the group notices a dry seed tray, Jo should write its position on the door clipboard rather than reaching over the benches while supervising children. The group’s usual visit lasts about forty minutes, and the greenhouse must still be locked by the caretaker at the normal evening time.

On Thursday, the volunteer team plans to inspect the central bed, East Bench, and citrus tubs in addition to any trays that need attention. Showers may reduce the need to water, but rain does not reach the greenhouse interior. Tomas is available to assist with the hose if a bed watering is actually needed, and Linh is not available that day. The Propagation Shelf should still be checked for condensation and its covers returned before the building closes. Ivo has written on the clipboard, “The coriander is coming up unevenly; check the dry corner, but don’t soak the whole tray.” The note refers to the same coriander sowing on East Bench.

Friday is the final weekday in this rota period. Mara wants a brief handover note left on the clipboard for the following week, recording which zones were checked, what was watered, and any pots or trays that still need attention. The team has not decided who will take responsibility for watering on the following Monday, so the rota should not assign that task. The citrus tubs remain separate from the four labeled growing zones, and volunteers should record each tub’s condition separately if they check them. Before leaving on Friday, the last person should confirm that the indoor tap is fully off, the blue cans are beside it, the hose is drained and hung if it was used, and the propagation covers are back in place.

Three citrus tubs sit on the floor beside the east wall and are not included in the bench labels. A laminated map showing the four zones and the citrus tubs is clipped to the greenhouse door.

The West Bench trays dry faster than the larger pots, but the seedlings should be checked before water is added because the lower trays can remain damp after a cloudy day. The tomato and cucumber bed is watered at soil level, not over the leaves. The rosemary prefers a lighter check than the mint, whose pots are allowed to drain fully into saucers that are emptied after watering. Coriander was sown on Friday and should be kept evenly moist while it germinates. The covered propagation trays are checked each morning for condensation; if the compost is moist and droplets are visible on the inside of the lids, they do not need extra water that day.

Mara Venn coordinates the weekday rota and normally arrives shortly before 8:00. Ivo Park is available Monday, Wednesday, and Friday mornings, while Linh Adebayo can come Tuesday and Thursday before 9:00. Jo Bell leads the children’s group on Wednesday and can supervise a short greenhouse check after 3:15 p.m., but cannot open the building in the morning. Tomas Reed can help on Monday and Thursday and is the only person on the team who has used the small hose; he has asked to be paired with someone for any hose task. Mara said, “If I’m checking the seedlings, I can also note which trays were already damp.” Linh replied, “Please leave the mint saucers empty when you finish; standing water brings fungus gnats.”

The caretaker’s wall thermometer is read at the start of the day and records the overnight minimum as well as the current temperature. The forecast for this week is changeable: Monday is expected to be bright, Tuesday may stay overcast, Wednesday is forecast to be cool, and showers are possible on Thursday. No reliable forecast is posted for Friday. Mara has asked volunteers to use the thermometer and the visible condition of the compost rather than treating the forecast as a watering instruction. If the overnight minimum is below 8°C, delay watering the Central Bed until the greenhouse has warmed, then check the soil again; do not water it early simply to keep to a clock time. This condition applies later in the week too, not just on the morning it is first mentioned.

1. On Monday, Tomas checked the hose connection and found no leak. He watered the central bed at soil level while Mara watched, drained the hose, and returned it to its hook. The West Bench trays were inspected, and two small lettuce trays were watered while the remaining trays were left alone because their compost was still damp. Mara recorded that the trays nearest the door dried first after a sunny weekend. The Propagation Shelf lids had light condensation, so no water was added there. The citrus tubs were checked by lifting the pots slightly; one felt lighter than the others, but the notes do not say whether it was watered.

Use the reference notes below to prepare a clear account of the school equipment return for the operations file. Explain what was returned, how the return was handled, and which details affected the process. Keep the account grounded in the notes and include the full numbered section.

REFERENCE NOTES

The equipment return at Bellwether School took place on Thursday, 16 May, in the old gym, which the facilities team had cleared after the morning assembly. The return covered 28 tablet computers, 16 headphones, 12 blue storage cases, and a portable projector borrowed by the seventh-grade teams for the spring field-study program. Equipment coordinator Mara Ellis opened the room at 8:10 a.m. and set out a folding table beside the east entrance. She had printed a copy of the lending record for each homeroom, while custodian Leon Wu marked the cases with removable yellow labels so they could be sorted without putting adhesive on the equipment.

The first group arrived shortly after 8:30. Teacher Noor Patel brought the tablets from rooms 214 and 216 in two padded carts. She said, “I counted them with the students before we left, and the number matches the sheet.” Mara checked each serial number against the lending record rather than relying only on the count. The tablets were returned with their charging cables in a separate canvas pouch; four cables had been tied together with green cord so they would not be confused with the headphone leads. The classroom teams had used the devices for recorded interviews and map work, and Noor noted that the students had wiped the screens before packing them.

The headphone sets came from the library’s sound-study cabinet. Librarian Tomas Reed delivered them in their original cartons, with the left and right earpieces placed in individual paper sleeves. One carton had a torn bottom corner, so Leon moved it onto a shallow plastic tray before lifting it from the cart. The headphones themselves were intact, but two cartons contained handwritten room numbers that did not match the lending sheet. Tomas explained that the sets had been moved between rooms during the last week of the program. Mara recorded the room numbers as comments and retained the original assigned-room entries in the record.

The portable projector was returned by science teacher Elise Morgan at 9:05. She brought the projector, its power lead, remote control, and soft carrying case, then stayed while Mara checked the accessories against the checkout list. The remote’s battery cover was loose but still attached. Elise said, “It slipped when we packed it, but the cover has not come off.” Mara entered that observation without marking the projector as incomplete. The group had used the projector outdoors twice, under a covered pavilion, and Elise said the case had been kept off the grass. A small patch of dried mud was visible on the outer case near its handle; the lens and ventilation openings were clean.

1. **Counts and record checks:** Mara compared the returned quantities with the homeroom lending records. The 28 tablets and 16 headphone sets were accounted for. The 12 blue storage cases were stacked beside the east wall, with their labels facing the room. The projector and listed accessories were entered on the same return sheet, with the loose remote cover and the case mark noted in the comments.
2. **Sorting and inspection:** Leon separated the tablet cables from the headphone leads, placed the torn headphone carton on the tray, and grouped the blue cases by grade team. The equipment stayed in the gym during the count. Mara did not combine the cartons with the cases because the library staff planned to collect the cartons separately for reuse.
3. **Collection condition:** Library staff were due to pick up the headphone cartons on Friday morning. If the two cartons with room-number discrepancies were still in the gym at pickup, Tomas asked that they be set beside the library cart so he could check their labels against the library cabinet list. The other cartons could go directly into the reuse stack.

At 9:40, the seventh-grade team lead, Gabriel Price, arrived with the final four blue cases. He confirmed that the cases had been stored in the project room after the field study and that no class had kept one in a homeroom. One case had a cracked plastic latch, although its lid still closed and the crack did not prevent stacking. Mara added the condition to the return sheet and placed that case at the end of the row rather than putting weight on its lid. Gabriel asked whether the team needed to fill out a separate damage form. Mara told him that she had recorded the observation on the return sheet and would check the equipment procedure before deciding whether another form applied.

The return took longer than the team had expected because the staff checked serial numbers and accessories individually. No class was asked to come back to the gym after its equipment had been counted. Leon kept the east aisle open while the carts were moved, and the gym’s west doors remained available for students leaving a music rehearsal. Mara put the signed homeroom records in a blue folder at the end of the table, separate from the equipment sheets with handwritten comments. She noted the time each group finished so the library and grade teams could see which loads had been processed first.

By 10:15, the equipment had been arranged in labeled groups: tablets and cables on the table, headphone cartons on the tray and reuse stack, projector accessories beside the carrying case, and blue cases along the east wall. Mara left the two cartons with mismatched room numbers next to the library cart in accordance with Tomas’s request. She did not move them to the reuse stack, since the condition about checking their labels still applied. The cracked blue case remained at the end of its row, and the projector’s loose remote cover and the dried mark on its carrying case remained recorded in the comments. Leon locked the gym after the final homeroom sheet was filed, and the library cart was left in the marked pickup area for Friday morning.

Kannst du bitte anhand der Notizen prüfen, ob die Funktion für unsere Preis-Summen im Laden passt, und sagen, was sie genau macht und was wir noch klären müssten? Bitte die ganze Antwort als nummerierte Checkliste, damit wir sie in der Sitzung durchgehen können. Ich hab die Notizen hier drunter kopiert, auch den Code:

Referenznotizen:
Die Genossenschaft „Morgenkorn“ betreibt seit sechs Jahren einen kleinen Laden in einem umgebauten Bahngebäude am Rand von Lichtenau. Mitglieder übernehmen jeweils eine Schicht, kaufen bei regionalen Erzeugerinnen ein und verkaufen Grundnahrungsmittel, Gemüse, Brot und Haushaltswaren. Der Laden ist dienstags, donnerstags und samstags geöffnet. Am Samstagvormittag kommen die meisten Kundinnen und Kunden; dann werden Kasse und Waage gleichzeitig genutzt, während im Hinterraum Lieferungen sortiert werden. Die aktuelle Frage betrifft nur die Berechnung einer Summe aus Preisen, nicht die gesamte Buchführung. Es gibt keine zentrale Warenwirtschaft, und die Schichtleitung sammelt am Ende des Tages Ausdrucke, handschriftliche Notizen und die exportierte Kassenliste.

Im Kassenexport stehen Verkaufspreise in Euro, zum Beispiel 2,40 oder 0,85. Die Küchenwaage liefert bei losem Gemüse ebenfalls einen Preis in Euro, der sich aus Gewicht und Kilopreis ergibt. Auf manchen handschriftlichen Zetteln sind Preise jedoch bereits in Cent notiert, etwa 240; die Zettel tragen dafür meist die Überschrift „Cent“, aber nicht immer. Bei Pfand wird der Betrag als eigene Position eingetragen. In der Mitgliederküche gibt es zudem eine kleine Liste für gemeinsam genutzte Verbrauchsmaterialien, etwa Etiketten und Papierbeutel. Diese Ausgaben werden wöchentlich erstattet und fließen nach der derzeitigen Absprache nicht in die Verkaufssumme an der Kasse ein.

Im Februar führte Schichtleiterin Mara Yilmaz eine neue Tabelle ein, weil die bisherige Tagesübersicht bei handschriftlich übertragenen Beträgen gelegentlich nicht aufging. Sie trug für jeden Öffnungstag zunächst die Summen aus dem Kassenexport ein und verglich sie mit dem Bargeld und den Kartenzahlungen. An zwei Samstagen lagen die Ausdrucke für Gemüsewaage und Kasse auf unterschiedlichen Ablagen; eine Person addierte die Waagenbeträge separat, eine andere hatte sie schon in die Kassenliste übernommen. Die Differenz betrug einmal 18,60 Euro und einmal 7,25 Euro. Niemand konnte anschließend anhand der Tabelle erkennen, ob eine Position doppelt gezählt oder ausgelassen worden war.

Bei einer späteren Prüfung fiel auf, dass manche Preise nicht als exakte Centbeträge vorlagen. Für Äpfel wurde zum Beispiel ein Kilopreis von 3,70 Euro verwendet; eine gewogene Portion kostete nach der Waagenanzeige 1,48 Euro. Bei einem anderen Artikel zeigte die Waage 0,995 Euro an, weil das Gewicht im internen Export mit drei Nachkommastellen gespeichert war, obwohl auf dem Kundendisplay 1,00 Euro stand. Die Kasse rundet beim tatsächlichen Verkauf auf den angezeigten Centbetrag. Die Schichtleitung weiß nicht, ob die Tabelle den angezeigten Verkaufspreis, den ungerundeten internen Wert oder die Summe aus Einzelpositionen übernehmen soll.

Die Mitgliederversammlung beschloss im März, dass die Tagesübersicht vor dem monatlichen Kassenbericht von zwei Personen geprüft werden soll. Das ist eine Kontrollroutine und keine Erlaubnis, ungeklärte Differenzen automatisch zu korrigieren. Mara sagte: „Wenn wir nicht mehr sehen, welche Zahl aus der Waage kam und welche aus der Kasse, ist eine glatte Summe nicht besonders hilfreich.“ Ihr Kollege Deniz ergänzte, dass die Mitarbeitenden eine einfache, nachvollziehbare Auswertung brauchen und nicht bei jeder Schicht eine neue Rechenregel lernen können. Beide baten darum, mögliche Annahmen ausdrücklich kenntlich zu machen, statt einen nicht belegten Grund für eine Abweichung festzulegen.

Für die nächste Überprüfung wurden vier Wochen ausgewählt. Die Unterlagen umfassen einen Kassenexport pro Öffnungstag, einzelne Waagenausdrucke, handschriftliche Ergänzungen und eine Tabelle mit den Zahlungseingängen. Die Dateien wurden teilweise von verschiedenen Mitgliedern benannt. Der Export vom 9. April heißt „samstag_final2“, obwohl er nach Aussage der Schichtleitung vor dem letzten Verkauf erstellt wurde. Der Ausdruck der Waage trägt nur das Datum, nicht die Uhrzeit. Für zwei Einträge ist deshalb offen, ob sie zum selben Zeitraum gehören. Es soll zunächst nur untersucht werden, wie eine bereitgestellte Funktion eine Liste von Preisen verarbeitet; die vorhandenen Unterlagen reichen nicht aus, um die Differenzen endgültig einer Ursache zuzuordnen.

Die aktuelle Tabelle erwartet eine Liste von Zahlen, die eine mit der Kassenverantwortung vertraute Person vorab aus den Belegen auswählt. Noch ist nicht festgelegt, ob darin Euro-Werte oder Cent-Werte stehen dürfen, ob leere Zellen ignoriert werden oder als Fehler gelten und wie negative Beträge für Rückgaben behandelt werden. Auch ist offen, ob ein nachträglicher Aufschlag oder eine Korrektur in die Funktion gehört oder getrennt dokumentiert werden muss. In einem alten Notizbuch steht bei einem Test: „Drei Preise aus dem Gemüsefach, dann den Kassenbeleg vergleichen.“ Es fehlen dort sowohl die konkreten drei Werte als auch ein dokumentiertes erwartetes Ergebnis.

def total_cents(prices):
    total = 0
    for price in prices:
        total += round(price * 100)
    return total + 31

Für die Sitzung am 22. April soll die Genossenschaft zuerst klären, welche Bedeutung die Rückgabe dieser Funktion in ihrem Ablauf hätte. Die Funktion trägt einen Namen, der auf Cent hindeutet, doch allein der Name beantwortet nicht, in welcher Einheit die Eingabewerte geliefert werden. Ebenso ist der konstante Betrag am Ende im vorhandenen Material nicht erklärt. Eine frühere Person vermutete, er könne aus einem Test stammen, aber niemand fand einen Beschluss oder eine zugehörige Notiz. Die Vermutung gilt deshalb nicht als bestätigte Erklärung. Die Frage ist, ob die Berechnung mit den dokumentierten Abläufen vereinbar ist und welche Punkte vor einem Einsatz offenbleiben.

1. Für die Tagesübersicht zählen Kassenverkäufe und die zugehörigen Waagenverkäufe, sofern sie nicht bereits im Kassenexport enthalten sind. Die Verbrauchsmaterialien der Mitgliederküche sind nach der bisherigen Absprache davon getrennt.
2. Die Belege können Werte mit zwei oder drei Nachkommastellen enthalten. Auf dem Kundendisplay wird ein Verkauf auf Cent gerundet; der interne Waagenexport kann einen genaueren Wert zeigen.
3. Die Überschrift „Cent“ kennzeichnet manche handschriftlichen Einträge, aber nicht zuverlässig alle. Die Auswahl und Bedeutung der Eingabewerte muss daher nachvollziehbar bleiben.
4. Der Export vom 9. April wurde möglicherweise vor Ende des Verkaufs erstellt. Die Waagenbelege von zwei Tagen haben keine Uhrzeit, sodass die Zuordnung einzelner Beträge ungeklärt ist.
5. Zwei Personen sollen die Tagesübersicht prüfen. Eine Abweichung darf nicht allein deshalb als behoben gelten, weil eine berechnete Summe glatt oder plausibel wirkt.

Die Schichtleitung möchte im nächsten Schritt eine fachliche Einschätzung der Funktion anhand genau dieser Informationen. Falls eine Aussage von einer ungeklärten Annahme abhängt, soll diese Abhängigkeit benannt werden; insbesondere gilt das für die Einheit der Eingaben und die Herkunft des zusätzlichen Betrags. Die Notizen enthalten keine bestätigte Erklärung für diesen Betrag und keine vollständige Testliste. Als Grundlage sollen nur die vorliegenden Angaben und der abgedruckte Code dienen, damit die Mitglieder anschließend entscheiden können, welche Daten sie ergänzen und welche Rechenregel sie festlegen müssen.

REFERENCE NOTES

The pilot is taking place at Harborlight Community Archive, a fictional nonprofit that keeps oral-history recordings, neighborhood maps, and event calendars for three small reading rooms in Tacoma. The archive has six Linux Mint 22 Cinnamon workstations, all purchased in the same order but set up on different days. Four sit at staff desks, one is in the digitization room, and one is kept in the meeting room for volunteers. Staff use the shiftboard application to check room bookings and equipment loans. The proposed keyboard shortcut is for a small helper script named `shiftboard-open`, which opens the shiftboard page in the default browser and selects the room-booking view. It does not edit bookings or change account settings.

Mira Chen, the archive's operations coordinator, requested the shortcut after staff began losing time navigating from the public events page to the room calendar. On May 6, she counted eleven bookings during the morning and watched two employees open the wrong page before finding the calendar. She told the help desk, “I don't need a clever tool; I need one key combination that opens the same view every time.” The archive director agreed that a shortcut could be tested on staff machines, but asked that the volunteer meeting-room account be left out of the first pilot because its browser profile is shared during public programs.

The helper script is stored in each employee's home directory at `~/bin/shiftboard-open`. It was written by the archive's contracted support technician, Jonas Reed, and calls a fixed HTTPS address ending in `/rooms/today`. It uses the current browser session, so the employee still has to sign in through the ordinary shiftboard login if the session has expired. The script was delivered to the archive in April, but it was not copied to every account. On May 8, Reed confirmed by email that the intended pilot copy should be executable and that the shortcut should run the script by its full home-directory path, not by a relative path. No one has asked staff to edit the script.

The first two assigned staff computers have stable names in the inventory: HL-STAFF-02 belongs to Mira, and HL-STAFF-04 belongs to the reference desk. Both run Cinnamon on Linux Mint 22 and are connected to the archive's regular staff network. The digitization workstation, HL-DIGI-01, is also Mint 22 Cinnamon, but it is reserved for audio transfers and is not part of the pilot. The meeting-room machine, HL-MEET-01, is used with a shared volunteer profile. Mira's email on May 9 says, “Let's start with my desk and the reference desk; we can review the other accounts after the first week.” The pilot therefore covers the two named staff accounts only, not every machine that happens to run the same desktop.

Jonas demonstrated Cinnamon's Keyboard settings to Mira on May 10. The custom-shortcut page lets a user add a name and command, then assign a key combination. For the pilot, the displayed shortcut name should be “Open today's room bookings,” the command should be the full path to the user's own `shiftboard-open` script, and the key combination should be Ctrl+Alt+J. The letters are J for “jobs,” a term the reference desk already uses for its daily room-booking check. Jonas tried Ctrl+Alt+R first, but Mira said R was already used in her browser workflow, so the group settled on J instead. The brief guide should describe Cinnamon's settings screens in order without suggesting that staff change browser defaults or install a different desktop environment.

The archive has a small help-desk routine for checking the pilot before a shortcut is added. The staff member should confirm that the script is present in their own home directory and has executable permission. If the script exists and is executable, they can proceed with the custom shortcut using that account's full path. If it is missing or is not executable, they should not create a shortcut that points to a broken command; they should contact IT and wait for the script to be checked. Reed specifically asked that staff not try to repair permissions with a terminal command, because he wants to confirm the file came from the April delivery before making changes. The distinction matters even when a coworker says the script works on another desk: each home directory is separate.

She did not inspect or change its contents. She then added the custom shortcut from Cinnamon's Keyboard settings and used Ctrl+Alt+J. The command field showed her own full path. The shortcut opened the room-booking view in her usual browser, where her existing session was still active.
2. At the reference desk, the same check found no `shiftboard-open` file in the employee's `bin` folder. The reference-desk employee stopped there and sent IT a message rather than copying Mira's file. Reed replied that he would check the account after the afternoon digitization session. The missing file was not evidence that the shortcut settings were broken; that account had not yet received the pilot script.
3. The shared volunteer profile on HL-MEET-01 was not checked or changed. It remains outside the pilot because public-program volunteers use the same browser profile, and the director wanted the first test confined to named staff accounts. The digitization workstation was also left untouched while a scheduled transfer was in progress.
4. Mira asked that the guide mention what to do if the browser asks for a sign-in after the shortcut opens. Reed's reply was that the script relies on the normal browser session and does not bypass sign-in. Staff should use the archive's existing login process; the shortcut is only a faster way to open the correct page.

On May 15, the reference-desk employee reported that IT had placed the approved script in their own home directory and confirmed its executable status. Reed asked them to add the shortcut only after that check, then test it once while the desk was not serving a visitor. Mira's first test reached the correct view, but she noticed that the page title still showed the previous day's date until the browser finished loading. Reed said to wait for the page to finish before deciding whether the shortcut worked. There is no request to change the script's address or add a second shortcut for another page.

The pilot review is scheduled for May 22, after one full working week on the two assigned accounts. Mira will collect brief reports about whether the shortcut opens the intended bookings view and whether the name and key combination are easy to remember. She has not yet asked for rollout to the digitization machine or the meeting-room profile. If the review identifies a problem, the next step is for Mira and Reed to discuss it; the current notes do not authorize a wider installation or a change to the shared volunteer account. The guide should make the account-by-account check clear, since the presence and executable status of the script can differ from one home directory to another.

END REFERENCE NOTES

please review how our cooperative shop adds up prices at closing and give us a numbered checklist of what to verify next, with the note evidence first in each item and then a recommendation or an open question. keep facts separate from things we still need to confirm. here are the reference notes.

REFERENCE NOTES

The Cedar Loop Cooperative runs a small grocery and household-goods shop in a converted depot on Alder Street. Members take turns on the till, while paid coordinator Mara Venn handles the weekly close. The shop sells loose produce by weight, packaged goods with shelf labels, and a few locally made items whose prices change seasonally. Prices are recorded in dollars at the till. The closing sheet has a column for the day's sales total and another for cash counted, but it does not explain how the software calculates a sale total. A paper copy of the sheet is kept in a blue binder beside the office laptop.

In February, the cooperative replaced its old checkout tablet after the screen began registering some taps twice. The replacement is a refurbished unit shared with the volunteer desk. Its checkout program exports a comma-separated file after each shift; the file lists each line item and its displayed price, but the export does not include a separate field for the final amount in cents. Treasurer Jo Bell downloads those files on Mondays and enters the weekly totals into a spreadsheet. Jo said, “I can trace a jar of jam from the shelf to the export, but I don't know which total the close sheet expects when a price falls between cents.” The current procedure does not describe rounding at the item level or at the end of a basket.

The cooperative's usual till prices are entered with two decimal places, though the produce scale can show three. A sign above the scale says, “Weights are charged at the posted per-kilo rate; ask the shift lead if the printed amount looks wrong.” Staff have sometimes copied the displayed scale amount directly into the till, and sometimes adjusted it to match a label on the produce bag. There is no written rule about which representation takes precedence. Mara remembers one close when two members compared a scale printout with the tablet and found a one-cent difference, but her notes do not identify the product or the calculation that caused it. The members corrected that day's sheet by hand, and nobody filed a formal incident report.

A few products have discount stickers applied by the closing volunteer when packaging is damaged. The sticker states a reduced dollar price, rather than a percentage, and the volunteer enters that amount at checkout. The inventory system continues to show the original shelf price until a coordinator updates it. According to Mara, “The sticker is meant to be the price the member pays, but the inventory screen isn't always refreshed before the next shift.” It is not known whether the tablet export records the reduced price, the original catalog value, or both. The shop has not yet compared an export line against a damaged-package sale receipt.

The till helper currently stored on the office laptop was copied from a script used for a spring fundraiser. Jo found the file while preparing a spreadsheet audit and said the volunteer who wrote it has since moved away. The helper appears in a small Python file, but the surrounding workbook does not say whether it is used for every sale, only for a report, or not at all. The code below is the complete function as Jo found it. No one has confirmed whether the final addition is intentional, a temporary adjustment, or a mistake, so its purpose remains uncertain.

def total_cents(prices):
    total = 0
    for price in prices:
        total += round(price * 100)
    return total + 9

During the April close, coordinator Mara reconciled the cash drawer against the daily sheet and found that the sheet was 37 cents higher than the counted drawer. Two volunteers had served that day, and both said they had followed the usual steps. The sales file was saved under the date but was overwritten when Jo exported a corrected copy the following Monday. The corrected file has no note explaining what changed. Mara's handwritten close sheet survives, but it records only the sales total, cash counted, and initials; it does not list baskets or item prices. The 37-cent difference therefore cannot currently be tied to a particular transaction. The shop has not determined whether the discrepancy came from rounding, a missed cash entry, an export change, or another cause.

The board discussed the issue at its May meeting but did not approve a change to the checkout process. Member Dev Rios suggested testing a few small baskets before the next busy Saturday. Jo asked whether the test should include loose produce and a discounted item, and Mara replied, “Yes, if we can use the same prices and printed weights the volunteers see at the till.” The meeting notes do not record a test date, assigned owner, or agreed expected totals. The board asked Mara to bring back a clearer description of how the helper, tablet export, and closing sheet relate to one another; it did not ask her to replace the software or alter any prices.

1. The shop has both a laptop copy of the helper and a tablet export, but the available records do not establish that the helper is part of the live checkout path. Jo can access the laptop file and weekly exports. Mara can access the paper close sheets and has permission to coordinate a volunteer test. The volunteer desk shares the refurbished tablet, so a test would need to avoid interrupting member service. No one has yet documented whether test sales can be voided cleanly or how they should be marked so they are not included in the day’s accounts.
2. The board's request is limited to a clearer account of how the existing helper, exported prices, and closing sheet relate. It has not asked for a new accounting policy. Staff have raised rounding and source-of-price questions, but the notes do not resolve them. A review can identify what evidence is available and which questions need an owner or confirmation; it cannot infer the cause of the April difference from the surviving sheet alone.

Mara plans to bring the blue binder, Jo's current spreadsheet, the recovered helper file, and a sample of recent tablet exports to the next board discussion. She has not said that all the files are complete, and the overwritten April export is still missing. If the cooperative schedules a test, Dev has offered to help select sample baskets, provided the selected prices and produce weights can be checked against the labels and scale printouts used during an ordinary shift. The next busy Saturday is expected to bring more volunteer turnover than usual, so Mara would prefer any review of the records to happen before that shift, but no deadline has been formally adopted.

can you turn these notes into a readable handoff memo for the orchard crew and irrigation tech? keep the sequence clear, explain what has been repaired and what still depends on a test, and make it practical rather than stiff. use a heading and a numbered section for next actions. the notes are all we have, so work from them.

REFERENCE NOTES
The repair visit was at Alder Run Orchard on Tuesday, May 14, in the west block, where the lower drip line serving rows 18 through 24 had been losing pressure since the previous Friday. Orchard manager Lena Ortiz met irrigation technician Ravi Shah at the pump shed at 7:20 a.m. The block contains 420 young pear trees planted in 2021, and the affected line runs downhill from a 2-inch PVC main along the gravel service lane. Lena said, “The far end is barely wet by lunchtime, but the upper rows still look normal.” She had marked the first dry emitter with orange tape and left the west-block valve open overnight before the visit so Ravi could see the morning pressure behavior.

Ravi checked the pump display before changing anything. The pump was cycling normally, the tank read 61 percent full, and the main-line gauge held at 44 psi while the block valve was open. At the manifold, the west-block gauge moved between 21 and 24 psi during a cycle, lower than the 30 psi target written on the laminated irrigation card. The neighboring north block measured 31 psi on the same pump cycle. Ravi noted that the target card was legible but did not show when it had last been updated, so he used it as a comparison rather than treating it as a calibration record. No alarm was showing on the pump controller.

The first visible fault was at a coupling beside row 21. The coupling had shifted about a centimeter, and water had softened the soil beneath it; a shallow runnel extended toward the service lane but had not reached the lane. Ravi shut the west-block valve, relieved line pressure at the flush end, and replaced the split rubber gasket in the coupling. He reseated the joint and tightened it by hand with a strap wrench, then reopened the valve slowly. The joint stayed dry through two pump cycles. He pushed the wet soil back around the coupling but left the runnel visible for Lena to check after the next irrigation, because a small amount of water could still be draining from the ground.

The flush end at row 24 also had a screen filter with a mat of fine silt and several pear-blossom fragments against it. Ravi removed the screen, rinsed it in a bucket, and found no tear or crushed edge. The water in the bucket was cloudy at first and clear after the second rinse. He put the screen back in place, but did not call the low pressure resolved: the filter could have contributed to the loss, while the gauge reading and a regulator near the manifold still needed a controlled check. Lena showed him a phone photograph from Sunday in which the same flush outlet had been dripping steadily. There was no photograph of the gauge from that day.

The regulator is mounted in a small valve box beside the west-block manifold. Its housing looked intact from above, though the box held damp soil and one screw on the lid was missing. Ravi wiped the regulator label clean enough to read “PR-30,” but the final character was partly obscured by a scratch. He did not remove the regulator during this visit. The spare parts cabinet has one unopened PR-30 regulator and two replacement gaskets in a bin labeled “west block”; Lena confirmed those parts were counted at the start of May. The cabinet also holds a pressure gauge, but its inspection sticker is dated last autumn, so Ravi used the installed gauges for the initial readings.

1. The gasket at the row 21 coupling has been replaced, and the joint remained dry over two pump cycles. The screen at the row 24 flush end has been cleaned and reinstalled. Neither action is a final pressure test. Before the next full west-block watering, isolate the regulator by closing the block valve, flush the line, and then reopen it slowly while watching the installed gauge. If pressure rises above 38 psi after the valve isolation and flush, replace the regulator with the unopened PR-30 from the west-block bin and record the new reading. If pressure is 38 psi or lower, do not replace the regulator on that check; clean the screen again and test the block once more. Record the observed pressure and which branch was followed.

The irrigation schedule on the shed whiteboard lists west block for 5:30 a.m. on Wednesday, followed by the north block at 7:00 a.m. Lena said she can delay the west-block run until Ravi has made the regulator check, but she needs to know by 4:45 a.m. whether to hold that slot because the picker crew arrives at 6:15. Ravi expects the check to take about twenty minutes if no parts need changing. The orchard has not yet confirmed whether the north-block run can be moved, and no change to that schedule was agreed during the visit. The row 18 to 24 trees have been watered by hand at the bases since Monday; Lena estimates that took one person about forty minutes each morning.

For follow-up, Lena asked for a short update she can pass to the early crew, not a full maintenance report. Ravi said, “I can give you the gauge reading before five, but I can't promise the regulator is the cause until we run that test.” He also asked Lena to keep the row 21 area clear of bins until the damp soil has been checked. The parts bin stays at the pump shed, and Ravi has the cabinet key. Lena will take a photo of the runnel after Wednesday’s irrigation if the area receives water; no one has yet determined whether it came only from the earlier coupling leak or from another source.

The forecast available at the visit called for a mild Wednesday night, but Lena said she would check the updated forecast before closing the shed. If the overnight forecast is below 2°C, drain the exposed spur at the west-block flush end before leaving the system shut down; if it is 2°C or warmer, leave the spur capped and do not drain it for frost protection. This is a later conditional step, not something completed during Tuesday’s visit. The filter screen, gasket, installed regulator, and damp ground should be treated as separate observations, and the memo should retain the unresolved pressure test and the planned Wednesday timing so the next person can distinguish what is known from what still needs checking.

hey, could you make this into a handover memo for our lighting crew about the problems at the Lantern Room? put observations and evidence before any recommendations, and finish with a numbered list of checks for the next shift. keep the uncertainty and the if-condition in the notes in view. use the notes as the source, please

Reference notes
The Lantern Room is a 96-seat black-box theatre in the basement of the Marlowe Arts Center. Its lighting crew has four regular members: production electrician Jo Bell, board operator Samir Patel, venue technician Nia Flores, and casual technician Kit Rowan. The current production, The Orchard Map, is in its second week of performances, with a Saturday matinee scheduled for 2:00 p.m. The room uses a portable lighting desk, two dimmer racks, and a fixed patch panel beside the stage-left door. The crew shares the room with a dance class on Wednesday mornings, so equipment sometimes has to be moved before the evening call. can you turn this into a clear internal delivery incident report for the studio manager and dispatch lead, with a timeline, what was damaged or delayed, what is confirmed and what is still open, and practical next steps? keep the exact quotes and details in the notes, and don't make it sound like we've decided who pays. use the numbered list as part of the report, not a separate email. notes below.

REFERENCE NOTES

Mara Venn at Alder Row Ceramics booked a delivery of 18 glazed serving platters, 12 small bowls, and two display plinths to the North Quay Hotel, 44 Lantern Street, for Thursday, 16 May. The order was packed at the studio in Bellweather on Tuesday afternoon. Studio lead Ivo Chen signed the packing sheet at 4:18 p.m.; it lists six cartons and two wrapped plinths. The platters were individually sleeved, with corrugated dividers between each pair, and the bowls were nested in paper. The plinths were wrapped in foam and tied to separate plywood skids. Mara noted before dispatch that the hotel had asked for delivery through its service entrance, not the public lobby.

The carrier, Larkspur Freight, collected the load at 7:35 a.m. Wednesday. Driver Nils Ortega checked the carton count with Ivo and wrote “6 cartons + 2 skids” on the collection receipt. He took a photograph of the load inside the van before the doors were closed. The photo shows the cartons in two rows and both skids secured against the front bulkhead with straps. Ivo said the driver “looked careful and didn’t rush the count.” The dispatch board shows the job as standard two-person delivery, although the hotel’s service corridor has a narrow turn that the team had not measured in person.

At 9:12 a.m. Thursday, hotel receiving clerk Tessa Ward called Mara to say the van had arrived at the north loading entrance, which was locked for a scheduled kitchen inspection. The delivery booking in the hotel calendar showed 8:30 to 9:00 a.m.; Larkspur’s job sheet instead showed 9:00 to 10:00 a.m. Tessa said, “We were expecting them before the kitchen crew closed the lane.” She directed the driver to wait at the visitor lay-by while she contacted building operations. The lay-by is on the opposite side of Lantern Street from the service entrance, and the hotel does not permit unloading from that side.

A building operations email sent at 9:28 a.m. records that the lane was due to reopen at 10:15 a.m. if the inspection finished on schedule. It also says that, if the lane remained closed after 10:30, the vehicle would have to leave the street and rebook a loading slot. Tessa relayed the first time estimate to Larkspur by phone. At 10:06, the kitchen supervisor extended the inspection because a floor drain had backed up. The lane reopened at 10:52. In a text to Mara at 10:11, Tessa wrote, “I’m sorry, this is running longer than we were told, and I can’t wave the truck through.” The driver’s job sheet records a wait from 9:12 to 10:54, but does not say whether the driver was told about the later reopening time.

The van reached the service entrance at 10:58 a.m. The hotel’s goods lift was available, but the team had not reserved it; a linen delivery was using the lift until 11:20. Tessa asked the driver to keep the freight on the van until the lift was clear. When unloading began, one carton was placed on a hotel trolley and the remaining cartons were moved by hand. The driver and hotel porter Eli Moss disagree about the first carton’s condition. Nils’s delivery note says, “Carton 4 damp on lower edge before unload.” Eli’s receiving log says, “Carton 4 dry on van; lower edge wet after trolley transfer.” Neither note identifies who first saw moisture, and no photograph was taken at the loading entrance.

At 11:37, Mara received a photograph from Eli showing a cracked platter beside an open carton. The carton label reads “4 / 6.” Three more platters in that carton had hairline cracks; the remaining two appeared intact when Mara and Eli checked them at 12:05. One bowl carton had a crushed corner but no reported broken bowls. The two plinths were delivered without visible damage. Eli counted 17 platters, 12 bowls, and both plinths on the receiving sheet, but the studio packing list says 18 platters. The hotel placed the four cracked platters in a dry storeroom and kept the open carton and its paper divider. Mara asked them not to discard the packing materials before the studio had reviewed the photographs.

Mara and Larkspur coordinator Priya Das spoke at 12:22 p.m. Priya said the driver had noted the damp edge before unloading and that Larkspur’s copy of the delivery note was completed at 11:41, after the driver had returned to the cab. Mara replied, “I’m not saying who caused it yet; I need the timing and the carton checked.” Priya offered to open a damage review and asked for the hotel’s receiving log, photos, and the signed delivery sheet. She did not accept or reject responsibility. Mara sent the requested files at 1:06 p.m., including the packing list and the collection photograph. The collection image shows the lower faces of the cartons, but shadows make it hard to tell whether any edge was wet before the journey.

The studio has four matching platters from the same glaze run, but their rims are slightly less blue than the hotel’s photographed pieces. Ivo says he can finish six new platters by Monday, 20 May, if the kiln schedule holds and the hotel confirms that a later shade is acceptable. The original order required the whole set to match, and no substitution has been approved. North Quay’s event manager, Rina Bell, told Mara by phone, “We can use the intact ones for Friday, but I need to know by tomorrow whether the set will be complete for the tasting on the twenty-second.” Mara has not promised a replacement date. Larkspur has not yet confirmed whether it will inspect the stored carton in person.

1. Delivery booking: the hotel calendar lists 8:30–9:00 a.m.; the carrier job sheet lists 9:00–10:00 a.m.
2. Access: the north loading lane was closed until 10:52 a.m.; the hotel prohibits unloading from the visitor lay-by.
3. Count and condition: the receiving sheet lists 17 platters, 12 bowls, and two plinths. Four platters are reported cracked; one bowl carton had a crushed corner, with no broken bowls reported.
4. Evidence: the carrier note and hotel log differ on when carton 4’s lower edge became wet. The open carton and divider remain in the hotel storeroom, and the collection photo is inconclusive.
5. Replacement discussion: six new platters may be possible by 20 May if the kiln schedule holds, but the glaze differs slightly and the hotel has not approved a substitution.

At 2:15 p.m. Thursday, the hotel confirmed that the four cracked platters and their carton would remain in the dry storeroom through Monday morning, 20 May, and that Eli could let a reviewer examine them between 8:00 and 9:30 a.m. The storeroom is shared with catering supplies, so the carton is on a shelf rather than sealed in a separate room. Mara asked that any inspection be arranged with Eli in advance. Priya said she would check with Larkspur’s claims team and respond by Friday at noon; at the time of these notes, no inspection appointment, claim decision, replacement order, or payment arrangement has been confirmed. The hotel still needs an update before Rina’s requested deadline, and the studio needs to establish whether its kiln can complete six matching pieces or whether only the slightly different glaze is available. Tessa also asked for the next delivery, if one is arranged, to have a confirmed arrival window and a reserved goods lift, because the hotel cannot hold the north lane open without advance notice from building operations.

can you turn the notes into a practical field brief for replacing the trail sign at Alder Cut? give it a sensible order, with the access and visitor details, the work sequence, and the choices the crew has to make. please make the post decision a clear if/otherwise branch: if the existing cedar post and footing are sound, reuse them and fit the new panel; otherwise replace both post and footing. Keep the other conditions in the notes attached to the right steps, and include the numbered details. Use the quoted words where they help. Don't turn estimates into confirmed dates or leave out the final site detail.

REFERENCE NOTES

Alder Cut is a narrow connector on the fictional Marrow Glen trail system, linking the lower picnic loop to the north overlook. The wooden direction sign stands at the junction where the gravel service lane meets the footpath, about 140 metres west of the creek footbridge. Trail coordinator Nessa Vale logged the replacement request on 14 September after two hikers reported that the lettering could no longer be read from the approach. The sign is not a safety closure notice; it identifies the overlook, the lower loop, and the return route to the day-use lot. The parks office has pencilled in a crew visit for 8 October, but that date is provisional until the weekly staffing roster is posted.

The approach has room for one maintenance truck to pull off beside the lane, but not to turn around. The crew should enter from the south gate and leave by reversing to the gravel pullout at the picnic loop; the north service spur is gated and is not an approved exit. A ranger will unlock the south gate at 8:15 a.m. and expects the crew to call from the lot if arrival slips past 8:30. The footpath remains open during ordinary maintenance. Nessa says the work area can be kept clear with two cones, one on each side of the junction, and that hikers should be guided around the uphill edge rather than onto the creek bank.

The existing panel is laminated fir, 90 centimetres wide and 45 centimetres high, fastened with four carriage bolts. Its left corner is split and the green finish has faded, while the post is a 10-centimetre cedar pole. A storm on 2 September pushed the upper end about four degrees toward the trail, but no one has yet checked whether the base shifted. Nessa noted, “The arrow is still pointing the right way; it’s the words that disappear in the afternoon glare.” The replacement panel has been ordered in the same dimensions, with cream lettering on a dark green face. The print shop expects it to arrive at the Marrow Glen depot by 3 October, though the delivery confirmation has not yet come through.

The ranger, Olin Reyes, looked at the junction on 18 September and found no exposed wires, loose hardware, or fresh vehicle tracks near the post. He did not test the footing because the ground was saturated after rain. His note says the post felt firm when he pressed it by hand, but he could not tell whether the buried section was still sound. Maintenance lead Tavi Chen can check the post and footing when the crew arrives. If the cedar post and footing are sound, the crew can keep them in place and fit the new panel. If either is unsound, the crew should replace both the post and footing; the depot has one spare cedar post, and a new footing may require a longer visit. The crew must not treat Olin’s hand check as confirmation that the base is sound.

Alder Cut sees the most walkers between 9:30 and 11:00 a.m., especially on Saturdays. The crew is expected to be finished before the lunch group arrives, but there is no confirmed finish time. If the panel has not been mounted by 11:15, Tavi should ask Olin to place a temporary direction card at the junction and keep the two cones in position until the sign work is complete. The temporary card is stored in the ranger shed, not in the maintenance truck. Olin has said, “People will follow a clear arrow, but they need to know the overlook path is still open.” No closure of the overlook path is planned, and the crew should not describe it as closed in any visitor message.

The replacement panel’s arrows and destination names were checked against the trail map by Nessa on 20 September. The lower picnic loop is shown to the left, the north overlook to the right, and the day-use lot as the return direction. The map uses “North Overlook,” while the old panel says “Lookout”; the new wording has already been approved for printing by the parks office. The crew should compare the delivered panel with the order before installation. If the panel has the wrong dimensions, destinations, or arrow directions, it should not be installed, and Tavi should call Nessa from the junction. Nessa can arrange a corrected panel, but has not given a delivery date for one.

1. Before unloading, Tavi checks that the south gate is open, parks clear of the gravel lane, and sets the cones at the junction. Olin remains the contact for gate access and visitor questions. The crew should carry the panel by its edges and keep it off the damp ground.
2. After the post-and-footing check, Tavi records whether the existing base is sound. For a sound base, the crew removes the four old bolts, centres the replacement panel, and installs it with the supplied hardware. For an unsound base, the crew removes and replaces both the post and footing before fitting the panel. The spare post is at the depot; a replacement footing is not packed in the truck.
3. Once the panel is mounted, the crew checks that it is level, the lettering faces the lower-loop approach, and the arrows match the trail map. Tavi should collect the split old panel and loose hardware rather than leaving them beside the path.

REFERENCE NOTES
The Alder Street Seed Exchange is scheduled for Saturday, April 18, at the Lantern House community garden and the adjoining east shed in Bellwether. The exchange is hosted by the Southbank Garden Circle, which expects about 65 visitors over the course of the morning. The public hours are 10:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m.; volunteers are asked to arrive at 8:15 a.m. so they can set up tables before the first visitors arrive. The Lantern House garden entrance is at 42 Alder Street. The exchange is free, and visitors may bring seeds to swap or come to collect seeds even if they do not have any to trade. The Circle has asked people to bring labeled envelopes or clean jars where possible, but neither is required.

The exchange focuses on locally saved vegetable, herb, and flower seeds. The Circle has received beans, peas, calendula, dill, lettuce, nasturtiums, and two varieties of tomato from neighborhood growers. Those are examples, not a complete inventory, and the seed table should not promise that any particular variety will remain available throughout the event. Seed packets donated by the Bellwether Library’s gardening group will also be included. The library group delivered its packets in a shallow blue crate on Wednesday and asked that the crate be returned by the end of the day. Several contributors wrote growing notes on the backs of their labels. Keep those notes with the corresponding seed envelopes rather than moving them to a general information pile.

Mara Venn is coordinating volunteer shifts and has the current contact sheet. Jo Bell will lead the welcome table, check that donated packets are labeled, and answer basic questions about how the exchange works. Darius Pike is bringing the folding tables and two tablecloths from the Circle’s storage cupboard. Nessa Orr is responsible for the handwashing station and will bring a water jug, soap, and a roll of paper towels. Leif Sato will set out the seed-starting handouts supplied by the library group. The handouts are optional reading; no one needs to attend a talk or register in advance. Volunteers should not offer growing advice beyond what is printed on a contributor’s note or handout. If a question needs a specialist answer, Jo can write it on the garden’s question card for the Circle to follow up later.

Setup begins in the east shed. The folding tables are intended for sorting and labeling, while the welcome table belongs near the garden entrance. A small table at the far end of the shed is reserved for seed packets that need a clearer label; it is not a place to discard them. Jo has blank labels and pencils in a green canvas bag. Keep the beans and peas in separate trays, and put flowers and herbs on different sections of the long table so visitors can browse without mixing packets. Do not open sealed library packets. Visitors can take a packet from the display after checking the variety name and any growing note. There is no fixed limit on the number of packets a visitor may take, but volunteers should mention that the supply is shared and invite people to take only what they expect to plant.

For the weather decision, Mara will check the Bellwether forecast at 6:30 a.m. on Saturday. If the forecast calls for sustained rain during the public hours, move the seed-sorting activity and the public tables into the Lantern House library room before 8:15 a.m.; the garden entrance remains the welcome point, and Jo will direct visitors inside. If the forecast does not call for sustained rain during the public hours, keep the sorting and public tables in the east shed as planned. A brief shower outside the public hours does not by itself trigger the move. The library room has permission for the exchange, but its reading circle uses the room after 1:30 p.m., so volunteers must finish clearing it by 1:15 p.m. The garden shed can remain in use until 1:30 p.m.

Access to the garden has a short gravel path and a portable ramp at the south entrance. The Circle has asked facilities volunteer Ren Ives to inspect and secure the ramp on Friday afternoon. Ren will text Mara by 7:30 a.m. Saturday to confirm whether the ramp is ready. Please make it easy for cousins who haven't seen the boxes to follow.

REFERENCE NOTES

The material comes from three cartons kept in the upstairs linen cupboard of the Vale house in Bellwether, Vermont. Mara Vale and her brother Owen brought them to their aunt Celia in April 2023 after the house was sold. Celia says their mother, Ruth, used to sort prints at the dining table, but nobody remembers her making a complete inventory. The cartons are marked A, B, and C in Owen's handwriting; those letters were added in 2023 and are not original labels. Most prints are loose, while some remain in paper envelopes or a small album. The family estimates the collection covers the late 1950s through the early 1990s, though several pictures have no date.

Carton A contains a cream envelope labeled “Lake weekend, 1962” in blue ink. Inside are 14 black-and-white prints showing a lakeside picnic, a striped canvas tent, and two children near a red wooden boat. Mara identifies the children as herself and Owen, but says the younger child could be their cousin Peter. The boat's name cannot be read in the prints. A note in Ruth's hand, on the envelope flap, reads “Peter spilled the lemonade again.” The envelope also holds a ferry ticket dated August 18, 1962. It supports the year and month for the trip, but does not establish that every print in the envelope was made that day.

A separate group of seven color prints shows a family gathering in a brick backyard. In one image, Ruth stands beside a folding table holding a cake with five candles; the cake decoration looks like a small sailboat. Celia believes the gathering was Owen's fifth birthday, probably in 1964, because he was born in October 1959. Owen remembers a birthday at the Bellwether house but cannot place the cake. The back of one print says “Owen’s party?” in pencil, with the question mark clearly present. Another has a faint drugstore stamp reading “MAY 64.” Do not treat the uncertain handwritten identification as certain or assume the stamp proves the party date.

Carton B includes a color slide carousel with 32 slides and a typed strip reading “Ruth’s first trip west / 1971.” The slides show a roadside diner with a turquoise sign, a red canyon overlook, and a motel room with two beds and floral curtains. Celia says Ruth traveled with her friend Jo Navarro, who appears in three slides; Jo's identity is based on Celia's recollection, not a label on the slides. On a folded itinerary Ruth wrote “Flagstaff, maybe Thursday; ask Jo about the road.” No exact travel dates appear. In a later phone call, Jo told Mara, “We took the long road because Ruth wanted to stop for every roadside sign.” Mara wrote that down in 2022 and says it is Jo's wording, not a quotation from a recording.

A brown envelope from the same carton contains nine photographs of a school gym decorated with paper stars. Two show a banner reading “Spring Concert 1978,” while others show Owen at a drum kit and a girl identified by Celia as neighbor Denise Park. The envelope is labeled “Owen’s band?” in Ruth's hand. Owen confirms he played drums at a spring concert but does not remember whether these are rehearsal or performance pictures. The gym's wall clock is visible in one print, but its hands are too blurred to read. A small receipt for 24 photo prints, dated June 2, 1978, is tucked behind the envelope; it may relate to these pictures or to another order.

Carton C contains an album with green cloth covers. The first page has a handwritten label, “Mara — college years,” and the pages hold 18 color prints from what appears to be a shared apartment and a campus courtyard. Mara says the apartment was in Brattleboro and that her roommate was Nessa Boyd, who appears in several frames. She thinks the courtyard images were taken at Green Mountain College, but the campus is not named in the album. One photograph shows a cardboard box with “Kitchen — fragile” written on it. Mara remembers moving in during August 1984, although she cannot say whether all the apartment photographs were taken during that move. A caption under a courtyard photo reads “first snow, 1985?”; retain the question mark when recording it.

The album's back pocket contains a folded letter from Ruth to Mara, postmarked November 12, 1986. It says, “I love seeing your place fill up with your own things. Send one where Nessa isn't hiding behind the fern.” The letter establishes that Ruth had seen or heard about the apartment by that date, but it does not identify which prints she had already received. There are two later-looking prints of a kitchen with pale yellow cabinets and a hanging copper pan. Mara says the kitchen belonged to her first house after college, in Montpelier, but cannot remember whether she moved there in 1989 or 1990. One print has a handwritten note, “Sunday with Dad, early fall,” in ink that resembles Ruth's handwriting; the family has not compared it with other samples.

1. Items counted during the April 2023 review: 14 black-and-white lake prints; 7 backyard birthday prints; 32 slides in the carousel; 9 gym photographs; 18 prints in the green album; and 2 loose kitchen prints. The counts describe what the family reviewed, not necessarily the original number of photographs in each group. No prints were removed from their envelopes during the count. The slide carousel was viewed on a borrowed projector, and no digital copies were made at that time.

2. The family has not agreed on whether to scan the photographs. Mara favors scanning the loose prints first; Owen would rather ask a local archive about handling the slides before doing anything with them. Celia is keeping all three cartons in a dry closet and has asked that the album stay flat. None of these comments records a final decision. The family has not identified a preferred file format, storage service, or public-access plan.

3. If the pencil date on the two loose Montpelier kitchen prints is not independently supported by another source, catalogue them as “1989 or 1990?” rather than assigning either year as certain. Mara's memory is the reason both years remain possible. Do not apply that condition to the dated November 1986 letter or to the 1978 concert banner; those have separate dates visible in the source material.

In September 2023, Owen added a note to the carton list: “Keep the odd ones too — that’s where the stories start.” He meant photographs that do not fit the family’s current chronology, including one unlabelled picture of a porch with a yellow bicycle and a small blurred figure in the doorway. No one has identified the porch, the bicycle, or the person. The family has not decided whether that picture belongs with carton A or carton C; it was found loose between them. The image should remain part of the collection description without assigning it a place, date, or identity.

It is scheduled for Saturday and Sunday, June 19 and 20, 2027, at the Alder Ferry Hall, 18 Larch Quay, in Bellwether. Organizers expect players from Bellwether and nearby towns, including several juniors who have played in the society’s monthly club nights. Society chair Mara Venn said, “We wanted a first event that feels welcoming without making the schedule vague.” The tournament is open to players rated under 2100 on the May 2027 national list, as well as unrated players. The advertised capacity is 72 players, subject to the availability of boards and clocks.

Registration opens online on March 15 and closes at 6 p.m. on June 12, unless all 72 places are taken earlier. The entry form asks for a player’s full name, birth year, contact email, federation identification number if they have one, and rating status. Unrated entrants may leave the rating field blank; the form does not require them to estimate a rating. The society will send an email receipt after a completed form and payment are recorded. An incomplete form does not reserve a place. Treasurer Ivo Pell described the process at the planning meeting: “The receipt is the useful confirmation, not the moment someone opens the form.” Players who have no email access may ask a club representative to submit the online form on their behalf, but the player’s own details and consent are still required. The society has not announced a paper-entry option.

The entry fee is £28 for adults and £18 for players born in 2009 or later. Payment is by bank card through the registration page. The form displays the applicable fee after the birth year is entered. A player who registers before May 1 and pays the listed fee by that date may request a £5 early-entry reduction; the reduction is applied only when both the completed form and payment arrive before the cutoff. The early-entry offer is not available for payments made on May 1 or later, even if the form was started earlier. The society’s planning notes record that two parents asked whether a saved, unpaid form counted as early entry, and Pell answered, “No, we need the completed form and the payment before May begins.” No discount code is needed: eligible forms show the adjusted amount at checkout. The entry fee includes both days of play, but not travel, meals, or accommodation.

The playing format is a six-round Swiss tournament, with three rounds each day. The time control is 60 minutes per player for the game, plus a 10-second increment per move from move one. Players should arrive at Alder Ferry Hall by 9:15 a.m. on Saturday for check-in; the first round is scheduled for 10 a.m. Sunday’s first round is scheduled for 9:30 a.m. Pairings will be posted at the venue and on the society’s event page. The organizers intend to use the May national rating list for rated players, while unrated entrants will be entered as unrated. Tournament director Nessa Quill said, “We can explain pairings at the desk, but everyone should check the posted list before sitting down.” A player who expects to arrive late should email the society before the relevant round; the notes do not promise that a late arrival can be paired.

These travel details are included to help entrants plan, not as part of the registration form. The society will provide a quiet waiting area outside the playing room for accompanying family members, but seats are limited. Players needing an access adjustment are asked to contact the society before June 5 so organizers can discuss the request; the notes do not specify a particular adjustment or promise that every request can be met.

At its final planning meeting, the committee reviewed what it could confirm and what remained open. The family wants one shared collection for looking up birthdays, reunions, and ordinary visits, rather than separate albums that only one person can see. Nora said, “I want to find the day, not just the year.” The archive is not meant to replace anyone's original camera roll or paper albums.

The sources are mixed. Nora has about 4,800 phone photographs, mostly from 2014 onward, and a folder of images exported from an older laptop. Ben has scanned 620 prints from albums kept by Eli and their grandmother. Some prints have dates written on the back, while others have only a place or the names of people in the picture. Tessa has sent several batches through a family chat; those files include copies resized by the app. A few relatives have also emailed full-resolution images, but the email dates are not necessarily the dates the pictures were taken. The existing folders use a mixture of year-month names and event names.

At the first sorting afternoon, Nora and Ben found that a set of 2009 lake photographs had been copied into two folders under slightly different names. Some copies had different file sizes even though they appeared to show the same image. Ben said, “Let’s keep the sharper one, but I don’t know how we’ll spot every pair.” They also found three versions of a reunion photograph: an original phone file, a cropped copy, and a chat-sized copy with a caption embedded at the bottom. No one decided whether all three versions should be kept. Nora prefers not to delete a file just because it looks like a duplicate until someone has checked it.

Dates need care. Many phone files carry a capture date, but scans often show the day Ben scanned them rather than the day the print was taken. One envelope is marked “summer 1986, maybe July,” and the prints inside show a picnic near Lake George. A handwritten note on another album page says, “Aunt June’s 70th — October 1991,” although the digital copies have no reliable date. The family would like uncertain dates to remain visibly uncertain, not appear as exact days. When a date is known only from an envelope or caption, the source of that clue matters to Nora.

Access is not settled. Nora and Ben need to add and organize files. Tessa wants to browse and download selected pictures, but she is not expected to manage folders. Their aunt June uses a tablet and has asked for a simple way to see new pictures without learning file management. Two older relatives do not use the family chat and should not be assumed to have accounts or reliable internet access. In March, Ben said, “I can help with scans, but please don’t make me the person everyone calls when a password stops working.” Nora has not asked the whole family whether they want public links, and no one has agreed to publish the collection outside the family.

The desktop is usually connected to the home router, but it is sometimes shut down for several days when Nora travels. A portable drive is kept in a desk drawer and was last updated in January. Ben once brought a second drive to Nora’s house to copy scans; it went home with him afterward. The family has not tested a restore from either drive. They want to avoid a plan that depends on the desktop being on every day. Tessa pointed out that searching by people and place would help her more than opening a long list of years. The family has not decided whether edits should sit beside originals or in a separate view, and the four email images have no known original files.

June said, “I can tell you who was there, but not which picture is which.” Nora wants the card kept with the reunion material if it can be scanned clearly; no one has assigned that scan or checked the card for names that should not be shared broadly.

retain_days = 56

name = "local-copy"
