input:
can you make this into a practical internal check memo for the shop lead? use the notes below, keep the actual readings and what people said, and make the follow-up clear. don't make it sound like a formal certification or claim we know more than the notes say.

REFERENCE NOTES

The ventilation check took place at Alder Street Woodworks on Tuesday, May 14, beginning at 7:20 a.m. The shop lead, Mara Venn, walked the floor with facilities technician Joel Park and safety coordinator Inez Cole. The shop was not running production during the first part of the visit, although the dust collector and the east-wall exhaust fan were switched on for the airflow checks. The outdoor temperature was 11°C, and the loading-bay door was closed except when materials were brought in. Mara said, “I want to know what changes when the big collector is running, not just whether the fan turns.”

The shop is a single-floor unit with a main cutting room, a sanding alcove, a finishing room, and a small materials store. The main exhaust fan is mounted on the east wall and has a variable-speed control beside the staff entrance. The dust collector serves the table saw, planer, and two floor drops; its start switch is near the planer. A separate make-up-air grille is above the north-side shelving. The finishing room has its own wall fan and a door that normally stays shut during spraying. The west roof damper was visible from the service ladder but was not adjusted during this visit. A handwritten label beside its access hatch reads “rain check before opening.”

With the dust collector off and the east-wall fan set to its usual marked position, Joel measured air movement at three locations using the shop’s handheld meter. At the main cutting-room aisle he recorded 0.42 m/s; near the sanding-alcove entrance he recorded 0.31 m/s; at the materials-store doorway he recorded 0.18 m/s. He repeated each reading once, and the second readings were within 0.03 m/s of the first. The meter was checked against its own zero function before use. Inez noted that a stack of plywood was partly in front of the make-up-air grille, with the nearest sheet about 20 centimetres from the grille face. Mara said, “That stack moves around, so please note where it was today.”

They then started the dust collector while leaving the east-wall fan at the same marked position. The cutting-room aisle reading fell to 0.34 m/s, the sanding-alcove entrance reading was 0.27 m/s, and the materials-store doorway reading was 0.16 m/s. Joel checked the readings again after about five minutes of operation; they remained within 0.02 m/s of those figures. The table saw and planer were not cutting material during this check, so the collector was drawing through the idle machines and floor drops rather than removing active dust. Inez wrote down that the collector made a low rattling sound for roughly ten seconds on startup, then settled to its usual hum. No one opened a duct or removed a guard.

The east-wall fan’s control dial has pencil marks at “usual,” “high,” and “service.” At the “high” mark with the collector running, Joel measured 0.39 m/s in the cutting-room aisle and 0.30 m/s at the sanding-alcove entrance. The materials-store doorway reading was 0.17 m/s. Mara pointed out that staff generally use the usual setting because the high setting is noticeably louder at the front bench. Joel did not measure sound level. At the usual setting, the fan grille had a light layer of dust along its lower edge; he did not clean it during the check. The grille was secure, and no loose paper or plastic was caught in it.

In the finishing room, Inez and Joel checked the separate wall fan with the door shut. A strip of tissue held near the door gap moved toward the room while the fan was running. With the fan off, the strip hung almost still. They did not take a meter reading in that room, and no spraying or solvent use took place during the visit. A small window was closed and latched. Mara said that the door is sometimes propped open while staff carry pieces through, but she could not say how often. The wall switch was labeled “FINISH EXTRACT,” and the fan ran without an unusual sound. The notes do not establish how the room behaves during spraying or with the door propped open.

1. Follow-up items recorded during the walk-through:
   - Mara will ask staff to keep the make-up-air grille clear and will move the plywood stack back before the next check.
   - Joel will inspect the east-wall fan grille and control at the next planned maintenance visit; no date was set during the walk-through.
   - Inez will ask the finishing-room users whether the door is commonly left open during work and add that information to the log.
   - The roof damper was left untouched. If the label’s rain check is relevant on the day of a future inspection, the team will confirm conditions before deciding whether to open it.

The team did not test the system during active cutting, sanding, or spraying, and they did not compare the readings with a specified performance limit. The figures describe the locations and operating conditions noted above, not every possible shop arrangement. Mara asked for the memo to distinguish what was measured from what still needs checking, especially the change in readings when the collector ran. Before leaving at 8:35 a.m., Joel returned the fan dial to its usual pencil mark, confirmed that the collector switch was off, and told Mara, “I’ve left the damper as we found it.”

North Quay Open registration file, assembled by tournament secretary Mina Voss on Tuesday, 14 April. The event is scheduled for Saturday, 2 May, at the Alder Street Community Hall in Bellhaven. The adult open begins at 9:30 a.m.; the junior section begins at 10:15 a.m. The entry deadline shown on the public form is Friday, 24 April, at 6 p.m. The club expects roughly 64 players, but that is a planning estimate rather than a confirmed entry count. Hall capacity is 80 people, including players, volunteers, and visitors. Mina said, “We can fit the boards in the main room, but the check-in table has to stay by the west doors.” The west doors are the accessible entrance and are also the route to the coat area.

The online form asks for each player's full name, club or school, age category, contact email, and requested section. It has separate options for the adult open and junior section, plus a box for an adult accompanying a junior. The form does not ask for a FIDE rating. On 10 April, Mina exported 41 entries to a spreadsheet and found two rows with the same email address but different player names. She has not determined whether those are family members sharing an address or a duplicate submission. Three forms list “North Quay Juniors” as the club, although that group closed last year; one of those players also selected adult open. Mina marked those records for follow-up but has not contacted the players. The spreadsheet has a column called “fee received,” but it is blank for 17 entries because payments are logged separately.

The posted fee is £18 for the adult open and £12 for the junior section. The form says payment can be made by bank transfer or in cash at the club desk by the deadline. Bank transfers should include the player's surname and section in the reference. Treasurer Owen Pike checked the club account on Monday, 13 April, and matched 22 transfers to entries; four more transfers had arrived without a clear reference. Owen wrote, “I can probably match the four if Mina confirms the player names, but please don’t mark them paid yet.” The club desk has recorded 11 cash payments on paper receipts, though two receipts show only a first name. The cash box is stored in the club office, not at the hall. No one has reconciled the paper receipts with the spreadsheet.

The advertised entry cap is 72 players, with a reserve list if entries exceed that number. A draft reserve list exists in a separate workbook, but it contains names from last year's event and has not been updated for this tournament. Mina says the list should be ordered by the time a complete entry and payment are received. The public form does not currently explain how ties in the timestamp will be handled. On 12 April, club chair Ravi Sen suggested that the committee “use the form timestamp, then ask the treasurer about payment status.” No committee decision is recorded. The entry count in Mina’s export is 41 submissions, but some submissions may need correction and several fees are not yet reconciled, so it is not a confirmed count of complete, paid entries.

For juniors, the registration notes say a parent or guardian must provide an emergency contact number and remain at the venue unless a named adult has been agreed in advance. The form collects an accompanying adult's name but not a separate emergency number. At the youth session on 11 April, volunteer Jo Bell said two parents had asked whether they could leave during the junior games. Mina replied, “We need to check the safeguarding wording before we tell anyone that is allowed.” No permission has been given for parents to leave, and no revised wording has been published. One junior entry has no accompanying adult named. The record does not show whether the player has a separate agreement on file, and Mina has not followed up yet.

The hall booking confirmation covers the main room from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. It includes 18 folding tables and 90 chairs; the club has 36 chess sets and 50 clocks available. Equipment coordinator Leila Hart counted the clocks on 9 April and found that seven need fresh batteries. She put those clocks in a marked crate and asked for batteries to be purchased, but the purchase has not been recorded. The club usually borrows extra clocks from the Bellhaven Library Chess Circle. Leila emailed that group on 13 April; its organizer replied, “I’ll check our cupboard after Thursday’s session.” There is no confirmation that the loan is available. The planned board layout has not been drawn, and the number of tables needed for the expected player count has not been checked against the hall arrangement.

A draft message is saved in the club drive, but its date still says “Saturday, 25 April,” and it promises a reply within two working days. The event date is 2 May, and the deadline is 24 April. Mina has not checked whether the draft has the correct junior instructions or a contact address for corrections. No confirmation email has been sent yet. Ravi asked whether the club should send payment reminders before the deadline; the notes contain no agreed schedule or approved reminder text.

He asked Mina for a final entry list by 7 p.m. on 24 April, but the public deadline is 6 p.m. Tomas says the extra hour is for resolving late spreadsheet updates, not for accepting additional entries. The notes do not say who will freeze the list or how a correction received during that hour should be recorded. Tomas also needs the players' names and sections, but has not requested their email addresses or payment details.

Mina is expected to manage the entry spreadsheet, but she is also listed to welcome visiting players. No one has been assigned to verify junior emergency contacts, answer payment questions during check-in, or take over the west-door table if Mina is away. The club has not yet circulated a final arrival-time note to volunteers.

The club's usual process is to keep entry records in the shared drive and retain paper receipts in the locked office cabinet after the event. The drive folder currently includes the exported spreadsheet, the old reserve-list workbook, the confirmation-email draft, and scans of some receipts. Access is limited to Mina, Owen, and Ravi, but Jo asked for a copy of the junior list to prepare check-in labels. No decision is recorded about whether that copy should include contact details. The club secretary says the registration review should identify the immediate questions for the committee before the deadline, while leaving unresolved policy matters clearly unresolved. The committee's next scheduled meeting is 20 April; Mina can bring urgent operational questions to Ravi sooner, but has not yet done so.
REFERENCE NOTES END

The album contains photographs from several branches of the family, along with a few pictures given to Mara by neighbors. Its original order was mostly preserved, although the pages were removed from their binding in 1998 for repair. Mara wrote dates and short descriptions in the album when she knew them; later pencil notes are in the hand of her nephew Owen.

The family remembers the house on Alder Street as a place where relatives gathered on Sundays. Mara’s brother David worked for the county road department and often brought home pictures from work trips, but not every landscape in the collection is connected to his job. Mara’s daughter, Elise, donated the album and loose prints to the Bellwether Historical Room in 2019. She said, “Mom always wanted the people named, but she didn’t want us making up the parts we couldn’t remember.” Elise can identify her mother and uncle in some pictures, but she was not present for the earliest events described here. The family has not established a complete list of everyone pictured.

On the back, in blue ink, is “Ruth and David, Mill Creek, July 1951.” The family has not confirmed which person is Ruth, and there is no note explaining whether Mill Creek is the road, the nearby waterway, or the community. The image is sharply focused, though the paper has a small stain beside the sign.

7. A color photograph records the 1976 Alder Street block party. A handwritten sign on a folding table reads “Bring a dish, bring a story.” Mara, identified by Elise, is serving lemonade beside the front gate. Three children are playing with a striped ball in the background, and none has been identified. The date “July 4, 1976” appears on the album page, not on the print. The front surface has a glossy patch where a clear album corner once covered it.

Elise’s caption says “last morning, October 1983.” A cardboard box and a rolled rug sit near the back door; the curtains are still hanging. No one is pictured. Mara kept this print loose inside the album’s back cover rather than attaching it to a page. The family would like the catalogue to help relatives recognize places and people without overstating what is known. Elise is willing to review name identifications, but has not yet reviewed a draft. The Historical Room’s staff hope the entries will be useful both to family members and to local researchers, especially people looking into everyday life around Alder Street. Mara’s captions are brief and sometimes uncertain, while Owen’s later notes are not always based on firsthand memory. The photographs should therefore remain connected to the words written beside or on them, including questions and qualifications. The final kitchen image is important to the family not because it documents a public event, but because it marks the end of a long period in the house. No account in the notes specifies what happened to the red thermos after the picnic.

Society volunteers kept the lobby open and brought in extra chairs; no one was turned away. Brooks welcomed the audience and explained that the filmmakers would introduce their own work, while the discussion after the screenings would be informal. He reminded guests that recording the audience discussion was not part of the plan, although the filmmakers had agreed to have still images taken during the introductions.

It followed the bus route between the college and the Riverside market, lingering on reflections in the windows and the changing light at three stops. Ruiz said, “I wanted the ride to feel like a place, not the bit between two places.” The piece used location sound recorded on two separate evenings; a brief announcement from the bus driver was left in, while a passenger’s name was removed from the final cut. During the questions, one attendee asked whether the route had been shortened for the film. Ruiz said no, and explained that the edit compressed two journeys into seven minutes without changing the order of the stops.

The second film, “Spin Cycle,” was a nine-minute fiction film directed by Malik Chen, a third-year student. It took place in a laundromat near the college and followed two siblings waiting for a washing machine to finish. Chen and the cast filmed on a Sunday morning before the shop opened to customers. The laundromat owner, Rosa Bell, let the group use the space on the condition that they cover the detergent labels visible in the background; the production team did so in every shot. Chen said, “The machines gave us a clock, so the characters didn’t need to announce how long they’d been waiting.” The society’s program listed the film as fiction, not documentary, because its dialogue and ending were scripted.

The third film, “Blue Hour, North Gate,” was a five-minute experimental montage by graduating student Leah Okafor. It combined still photographs and moving images of the North Gate plaza, including footage shot from the second-floor walkway during a light rain. Okafor said she had asked campus facilities for permission before using a tripod there, and that the crew stayed behind the marked line near the stairwell. A few audience members recognized the plaza from the college’s old library entrance, which closed for renovation in 2022. Okafor said, “I kept the old sign in the frame because people still use it when they give directions.” The film had no spoken dialogue; its soundtrack was made from recordings of rain, footsteps, and a gate latch.

   - 7:31 p.m.: “Blue Hour, North Gate” began.
   - 7:40 p.m.: the audience discussion started and ended at 8:03 p.m.

The conversation included questions about sound, permission, and how a short film can suggest a longer routine. A student in the front row asked whether filming everyday places risked making their regular users into scenery. Patel answered, “That’s a fair question; we tried to let each filmmaker explain what they chose to show and what they left out.” Ruiz described removing the passenger’s name, and Chen discussed Bell’s request about the detergent labels. Okafor spoke about checking where the tripod could stand. Brooks noted that the society had invited the campus accessibility coordinator to review the entrance arrangements after the delay, but no review had taken place yet. The coordinator’s visit was pencilled in for the following week, subject to their schedule.

Several practical details came up afterward. The society handed out 58 programs and counted 64 attendees, including the three filmmakers and four volunteers. The count was made at the door and was not a registration total. The event used the society’s portable subtitle screen for the opening remarks, but none of the three films had captions. Patel wrote down a request from two audience members for captions at future screenings. The team had not yet chosen its next program, and Brooks said the society would discuss possible themes at its regular meeting on April 25. No date or title for another public event had been announced.

The room setup had been checked at 5:50 p.m. by volunteer Jamie Park, who found that the projector picture was slightly out of focus. Park adjusted the focus ring, but the image softened again when the projector warmed up. At 6:03 p.m., technician Ellis Ward joined Park to check the lens and the wall screen. The society had not yet replied to that note.

reference notes

The luggage desk at North Quay serves the evening ferries operated by Alder Line. On 14 September, the desk was staffed by Mara Venn and Olin Pike from 16:00 until the last scheduled arrival. The desk sits beside the covered ramp, opposite the ticket window; bags waiting for collection are kept in a locked cage behind the counter. The late ferry, the Larkspur, was due at 19:20 but tied up at 19:47 after a warning light required a check in the harbor. The waiting area stayed open, and the desk did not close during the delay. A paper board outside showed the revised arrival time, while the terminal’s public display continued to show 19:20 until 19:35.

At the start of the shift Mara counted 23 tagged items in the cage and Olin checked the paper ledger against the handheld scanner. They agreed that the ledger was the working record if the scanner froze, because the scanner had dropped its connection twice the previous evening. The green claim stubs used on the Larkspur had a four-digit number and the sailing date printed in the upper right corner. Each bag tag had the same number, written in large black figures, and a small blue Larkspur mark. The desk also handled items from the earlier Rowan sailing, whose tags used a red mark; the different color was useful but was not a substitute for checking the sailing and number. Mara said, “Let the number do the talking, but check which boat it belongs to.”

The desk rule discussed at shift handover was this: if a passenger presents the paper claim stub and its four-digit number and sailing date both match the bag tag and ledger entry, staff may release the bag after asking the passenger to sign the collection column. If the passenger has no stub, or either the number or sailing date does not match, staff must not release the bag; they must write the details in the amber discrepancy log, leave the bag in the locked cage, and refer the case to the supervisor. The two conditions in the first branch have to match together; a match on the number alone is not enough. If the supervisor is away from the desk, the staff member should call the on-duty terminal lead and keep the bag secured until the supervisor or lead gives instructions. Mara made clear that a passenger’s confidence or a familiar-looking bag does not replace the check.

A family collecting two suitcases from the Rowan had one green Larkspur stub among its papers. Olin noticed the red Rowan marks on both bags and checked the ledger rather than assuming the green paper belonged to them. The Rowan numbers were 3186 and 3191; the green stub showed 3186 but listed the Larkspur and the later sailing date. The family’s other Rowan stub showed 3191 with the correct date. Olin released the suitcase whose red tag, stub and ledger entry all matched, and recorded the signature. He did not release the other suitcase. He entered the mismatch in the amber log, put the suitcase back in the cage, and explained that the supervisor would review it. The family left with the matching case and a note of the desk’s closing time.

At 18:55 a passenger named Tessa Vale came to ask about a small canvas instrument case, saying she had left it on the Larkspur before it sailed from Bell Quay. There was no claim stub in her wallet. A deckhand had brought the case to the desk, and its tag read 4402, but the paper ledger listed 4407 against the same description. Mara did not release it, even though Tessa recognized a silver tape mark on the handle. She wrote Tessa’s name, the two numbers, the sailing date and the description in the amber log, then secured the case in the cage. The supervisor had gone to check a queue at the vehicle ramp. Olin called the on-duty terminal lead, who asked them to leave the case secured and pass the entry to the supervisor on return. Tessa was told what had been recorded and that the desk could not hand it over before review.

1. For every collection, compare the claim stub with the tag and ledger, including both the four-digit number and the sailing date. Record the passenger’s signature in the collection column only after the checks match. Use the red or blue sailing mark as an additional clue, not as the only check.
2. If the stub is missing, or either printed detail does not match, do not release the item. Enter the discrepancy in the amber log, return the item to the locked cage, and refer the case to the supervisor. If the supervisor is away, call the on-duty terminal lead and keep the item secured while waiting for instructions.
3. When the scanner is unavailable, use the paper ledger as the shift’s working record and compare it with the physical tag and stub. Note any scanner problem for the next shift; do not treat a scanner failure as permission to skip the comparison.

The next evening shift was due to start at 20:00, after the Larkspur’s late arrival. Before handing over, Olin wrote the total cage count as 24, noting that the instrument case had been added after the initial count of 23. He left the amber log open at Tessa Vale’s entry and told the incoming clerk that the supervisor had not yet reviewed it. The family’s unresolved Rowan suitcase remained in the cage as well. The terminal lead had not authorized release of either item; the lead’s instruction was to keep the cases secured until the supervisor reviewed the entries. Mara put the paper ledger, green and red sample tags, and scanner on the desk shelf so the incoming clerk could see which records and marks had been used. The public display had returned to the correct arrival time, but the board outside still showed the delay notice, so Olin left both displays in place until terminal operations updated the board.

The handover is meant for staff taking over during a busy arrival period, not for passengers. Mara and Olin wanted the next clerk to know which bags were already cleared, which remained under review, and why a tag color alone could not settle a claim. Their final note said, “Keep the two held items in the cage, and leave the amber entries for the supervisor.” It also recorded that the Larkspur’s delay had not changed the collection check or the requirement to keep an unmatched item secured. No one at the desk had told the family or Tessa that either held item would definitely be released after review.

can you turn this into a prompt for an internal warranty review by the service team? have them assess whether the washer repair may qualify, and what still needs checking. make it a numbered checklist, with the evidence before each recommendation. if the facts aren't enough, don't force a final coverage decision. use these notes:

REFERENCE NOTES
The appliance is a Bracken & Vale front-loading washer, model WN-640, serial number BV64-19-88317. Customer Mira Solis bought it from North Quay Home Supply on 18 September 2024 for $879 before tax. The order confirmation lists standard delivery to 44 Larkspur Court, Unit 3, Bellwether. Delivery and installation took place on 21 September. The retailer's work order says its crew leveled the washer, connected the hot and cold supply lines, ran a short rinse, and observed no leak at that time. The customer says the crew reused a braided inlet hose already at the apartment; the crew's job sheet does not identify who supplied that hose. The original receipt, delivery record, and job sheet are in the case folder.

The warranty card supplied with the washer states a two-year limited warranty for parts and labor beginning on the purchase date. It says defects in materials or workmanship may be repaired or the affected part replaced after inspection by an authorized service provider. It excludes damage caused by improper installation, misuse, or external conditions. The card says the customer must provide proof of purchase and make the appliance accessible for inspection. It does not promise a particular repair date and does not state that a prior service visit automatically approves later claims. The customer registered the appliance online on 20 September 2024. The registration email confirms the model and serial number but shows the purchase date as 19 September, one day later than the receipt.

Mira first contacted Bracken & Vale support on 6 February 2026. She reported that the washer had stopped during a normal cotton cycle and displayed code E17. She said there was a small amount of water on the floor behind the left rear corner, but she did not see water inside the drum after stopping the cycle. She unplugged the washer and closed both wall shutoff valves. Support agent Leon Park recorded the call and advised her not to run another cycle until the water source was checked. His note says the appliance had been in its current location since delivery and had not been moved or repaired. Mira later clarified that she had cleaned the detergent drawer in January, using a damp cloth, and had not removed the rear panel or altered the plumbing.

A service visit took place on 10 February. The authorized technician, Hana Bell, found dried mineral marks near the cold-water inlet connection and moisture on the floor, but no active leak while the supply valves were closed. She did not run a full wash cycle because the building manager could not confirm that the floor below was protected from possible water escape. Bell photographed the rear panel, hose connections, and the serial label. Her report says the hose looked worn near its metal coupling, but she could not determine whether that wear caused the reported leak. The inlet valve was not removed or bench-tested. Bell noted that E17 can appear when the washer detects an unsuccessful water fill, but the code alone does not identify a failed part. Her estimate listed a diagnostic follow-up, a replacement inlet hose if needed, and possible testing of the inlet valve; it was not an authorization to replace parts.

The technician's photographs show a braided hose with a blue stripe on the cold-water side. The outer braid is flattened for about two centimeters close to the coupling, and there is light green residue on the washer-side thread. The corresponding hot-water hose has no visible flattening in the available image. The photographs do not show the wall-side connections clearly, and the serial-label image is legible. Bell did not record the hose's age, manufacturer, or purchase source. The customer has since found a hardware-store receipt dated 3 August 2023 for two braided washer hoses, but the receipt does not give hose model numbers and does not say which property they were used at. Mira says she believes the hose in the photograph came from that pair, but she cannot confirm it from the receipt alone.

On 12 February, Mira emailed support that she had seen a brief drip in November 2025, wiped it up, and then used the washer normally without seeing another puddle until February. She had not called at the time because she thought water had come from a wet raincoat on the floor. She says the washer has been used about four times a week, mostly on cold or warm settings, and that she uses the detergent amount printed on the bottle. A building maintenance note records a plumbing inspection in October 2025, but it concerns the kitchen sink and does not mention the laundry connections. The building manager, Ellis Ward, wrote that there was no reported leak in the apartment below before 6 February; the apartment below was vacant from 15 January to 2 February, so that period was not continuously observed.

The service team has not received a full-cycle video, a test result for the inlet valve, or a second inspection of the hose while connected. No one has confirmed whether the wall shutoff valves or the hose coupling are leaking under pressure. The customer has kept the removed detergent drawer but says she has not disconnected the hoses. The washer is still unplugged, and the water valves remain closed. Mira is available for another visit after 16:00 on weekdays and says the building manager can provide access to the laundry closet if given one day's notice. Her preferred contact is email, although she accepted the initial visit by phone.

1. 18 September 2024: retailer receipt for model WN-640, serial BV64-19-88317, purchased by Mira Solis; total before tax $879.
2. 21 September 2024: delivery work order records leveling, supply-line connection, and a short rinse with no observed leak; hose supplier is not identified.
3. 6 February 2026: support call records E17 during a cotton cycle, water behind the washer, and advice to stop using it and close the supply valves.
4. 10 February 2026: authorized visit records dried mineral marks, moisture, a worn-looking hose coupling, and no confirmed source or tested inlet valve.
5. 12 February 2026: customer email reports a possible earlier drip in November 2025 and identifies a 2023 hose receipt without a model number or property details.

Bell's report includes the following ordinary observations: “The cold-side hose appears compressed close to the washer coupling.” It also says, “I cannot tell from the visit whether the hose, inlet valve, or a connection at the wall is responsible.” In her email, Mira wrote, “I want to know whether the warranty could cover the repair before I agree to any paid parts.” She also wrote that she is willing to make the washer available for testing but does not want it operated until the leak risk has been checked. These statements record what the technician and customer said; they do not establish the cause of the leak or the warranty outcome.

One condition in the warranty card may matter to a later assessment: if an authorized inspection confirms that damage was caused by improper installation, the card excludes that damage; if inspection instead identifies a defect in a washer part, the stated parts-and-labor coverage may be relevant, subject to the card's terms. Neither condition has been confirmed in this file. The difference between the receipt and online-registration purchase dates also remains unexplained, although both records identify the same model and serial number. No replacement part has been approved, no repair has been completed, and the customer has not accepted the estimate. The file contains no final coverage decision.

Families can bring items to the library desk between 8:15 and 3:30 on school days. The main entrance opens at 8:00, but the library desk is not staffed before 8:15. Equipment should be returned by the student or an adult listed as an authorized contact. The school has not asked students to leave devices unattended outside the library.

The loan pool includes Chromebooks, padded sleeves, power adapters, and a small number of wireless mice. Each item has a Cedar Grove inventory sticker, usually on the underside or inside flap. The Chromebook number is also printed on its login card. Some families received a sleeve and adapter together, while others received only a Chromebook. A mouse was optional, not part of every loan. The family’s issue sheet, sent home in September, lists the items assigned to that student; the office can look up the list if the sheet is missing. Students should not write their passwords on the issue sheet or put them inside the device sleeve.

At the library desk, staff will check the inventory sticker against the return log and look for the issued accessories. They will make a brief visual check for obvious damage, but the desk check is not a repair assessment. Families do not need to erase files or sign out of the school account before returning a Chromebook. Staff will handle account sign-out after intake. A cracked corner, loose hinge, or screen mark should be mentioned at the desk so it can be noted accurately; reporting damage is not, by itself, a statement about who caused it. One parent said, “I can bring the Chromebook, but I’m not sure where the little charger went.” The librarian replied, “Bring what you have, and we’ll compare it with the issue sheet.”

The return log has separate boxes for “received,” “accessory missing,” and “needs follow-up.” Staff should not mark a set complete just because the Chromebook is present.    If a family brings the assigned equipment to the staffed library desk by 3:30 p.m. on Friday, May 22, staff should check the inventory and accessories there and record what is physically received. If the family cannot come during the library desk hours, they may place the equipment in a closed bag with the student’s name and grade written on the outside and take it to the main office before 4:00 p.m. on May 22. In that alternative case, office staff should give the bag to the library team for checking on the next school day; the office receipt is not confirmation that every assigned item is inside. Do not direct families to leave equipment at the entrance or put it in the library’s after-hours book slot, which is for books only.

On Tuesday morning, May 19, the library team tested the return log with two sample records and found that the accessory boxes were easy to overlook on a phone screen. They enlarged those fields and added a prompt for the staff member to read the assigned-item list before closing an entry. The team plans to use the revised log throughout the return window. The office copier is available for extra issue sheets, but staff should first check whether a family needs a replacement rather than automatically printing one. A guardian asked, “Do we need to wait while you test the whole computer?” The desk aide answered, “No, we check the sticker and the outside here; technical checks happen later.” Keep that distinction clear so a quick intake is not described as a full device test.

2. Dates, follow-up, and communication
   The school sends a reminder through its family portal on May 15 and a final reminder on May 21. The reminders should say where and when to return equipment, what to bring if available, and how the alternate office drop-off works. They should not claim that every student received every accessory. A family that cannot locate an item can still return the other assigned equipment during the window and speak with staff about the missing item. If a family needs language assistance, the office can arrange a call with the school’s interpreter service; families should contact the main office rather than write private student information in a public message thread. The general office number on the school calendar is the appropriate contact route.

If the library team finds a discrepancy after a bag has been left at the office, it should contact the listed adult using the school’s usual private communication channel and describe only the item that needs clarification. It should not tell a student in a hallway that the family owes money or has lost school property. The notes do not establish a fee, replacement charge, or consequence for any missing or damaged item, and the return guide should not imply one. The school wants accurate records and a straightforward way for families to ask questions; it has not announced a decision about individual cases. When a family later brings an item shown as missing on the reminder slip, staff should update the existing log entry rather than start a duplicate record.

After the May 22 window, the school will review the intake log and contact families only where an assigned item still needs clarification. No one should promise that a device will be available for a particular student next term, because next year’s assignments have not been made. The guide can explain that the library team will check returned equipment after intake and that families may be contacted about a recorded discrepancy. Keep the description modest: staff can confirm what was handed in and what still needs follow-up, but they should not present a visual desk check as proof that a device works. The purpose of the guide is to help families complete the return, understand the two drop-off routes, and know what to expect if an accessory is not there. End with the school’s general office contact route for questions, without adding a new deadline or making a promise about a specific case.

Please prepare a clear, reader-friendly overview of the latest community survey export for the Rivermill Neighbourhood Partnership. Use the reference notes below as the complete source. Organize the information so residents and partner organizations can understand when the survey ran, who responded, what the results show, and how the export should be interpreted. Keep reported figures and quotations accurate, distinguish observations from explanations, and do not infer causes that the notes do not establish. Include a numbered section for the practical details of the export. Copy the full reference-notes block into your response unchanged after the overview.

REFERENCE NOTES

The Rivermill Neighbourhood Partnership conducted its spring community survey from April 8 through May 19, 2025. The partnership serves the east and central parts of Rivermill, a fictional town of about 31,000 residents beside the Alder River. The survey was available online and on paper in English and Spanish. Paper copies were placed at the public library, the Northgate market, and the Mill Street health centre. Volunteers also brought copies to two Saturday events at the riverfront hall. The partnership received 486 submissions. After removing 17 blank forms and 9 duplicate submissions, the export contains 460 responses. The project coordinator, Lena Ortiz, said, “We wanted to hear from people who do not usually come to our evening meetings, not just add another meeting to their week.”

The export records answers to 22 questions, along with a small set of optional background questions. Questions covered access to parks, local transportation, street lighting, flood preparedness, and preferred ways to receive partnership updates. Respondents could skip any question. As a result, the number of answers varies by question; the total of 460 applies to included survey submissions, not to every chart or item. The export includes a response-count field beside each question’s results. The partnership did not collect names, street addresses, or email addresses in the survey form. A separate sign-up sheet at the riverfront events was not part of the export and should not be described as survey data.

1. Export and collection details
   - The file was prepared on June 3, 2025, by data volunteer Priya Nair, using the partnership’s standard spreadsheet template.
   - It contains one row per included submission and one column for each survey question or recorded category. The first row contains column headings; the response records begin on the second row.
   - The original paper responses were entered by two volunteers and checked by a third person against the paper forms. The online responses were downloaded from the survey platform on May 21.
   - The export uses “Prefer not to say” when that option was selected, and leaves a response cell empty when a participant skipped the question. Those two situations must not be treated as the same answer.
   - Before sharing the file with partner organizations, the team removed free-text comments that named a specific person or gave a precise home address. The remaining comments were not edited for style.

For the park-access question, 438 respondents selected an answer. Of those, 194 said they could reach a public green space within a 10-minute walk, 152 selected 11 to 20 minutes, and 92 selected more than 20 minutes. Another 22 submissions skipped the question. The Northbank and Mill Street areas had the largest number of respondents in this item, but the export does not contain population-based weights, so those counts do not show the share of all residents in either area. In an open comment, one respondent wrote, “The little path behind the old depot is lovely, but the gate is hard to open with a stroller.” The partnership has not verified the path condition or assessed the gate as part of this survey.

Answers about transportation showed that 171 of 421 people who answered the item selected bus service as the local issue they most wanted addressed. A further 126 chose safer walking routes, 74 chose bicycle connections, and 50 chose another listed option. Thirty-nine respondents skipped the item. In a separate question about getting to evening appointments, 118 respondents said they had missed or rescheduled an appointment in the past year because of transportation; 287 said they had not, and 31 preferred not to say. The survey did not ask what kind of appointment people attended, and these figures are self-reported. At the May 10 riverfront event, volunteer Mateo Ruiz said, “Several people asked whether the survey would be read before the bus schedule is reviewed.” His comment is a record of what he heard at that event, not a finding from a separate interview study.

The street-lighting question received 447 answers. A total of 203 respondents described lighting on their usual route as good or very good, 139 chose fair, and 105 chose poor or very poor. Thirteen submissions skipped the question. The survey did not ask respondents to identify individual poles, and the export has no inspection records or measured light levels. The partnership’s facilities liaison, Anika Bell, noted that the town had replaced 18 lamps on Cedar Avenue in March, before the survey opened. That maintenance detail is included as background, not evidence that the replacement caused any particular survey response. The comments included one resident’s remark, “The crossing by the laundromat still feels dark when it rains.”

Flood-preparedness answers were more varied. Of 432 people who answered, 238 said they knew where to find local flood guidance, 149 said they did not, and 45 selected “Prefer not to say.” Twenty-eight skipped the question. The survey did not test whether respondents could recall a particular emergency step, and a yes answer should not be presented as proof of preparedness. The partnership shared a printed flood-information card at the library beginning April 22, midway through the survey period. The export does not identify when each person completed the survey, so the responses cannot show whether seeing that card changed anyone’s answer. During a volunteer debrief, Jo Park said, “The map at the library was easier to follow after they put the bus stop names on it.” This is an attributed comment from the debrief, not a survey response.

Preferred update channels were selected by 451 respondents, who could choose more than one option. The results therefore count selections rather than unique people within each channel: 276 selected email, 198 selected printed notices at local venues, 146 selected text messages, and 83 selected the partnership’s website. Selections add up to more than 451 because multiple answers were allowed. Nine submissions skipped the question. The partnership currently sends a monthly email bulletin and distributes printed notices through six venues; it does not yet send text alerts. These existing practices are context from the partnership office and are not measures of how often residents read each channel. No respondent was automatically subscribed to any update list by completing the survey.

The figures in this export describe people who chose to submit a survey, rather than a random sample of Rivermill residents. The partnership did not calculate a margin of error or claim that the response mix matches the town’s population. A separate neighborhood comparison is possible only when enough responses are available to protect privacy and avoid over-reading very small groups. If a neighborhood has fewer than five answers for an item, do not show a neighborhood-only figure for that item; retain the relevant answers within townwide totals where appropriate. This condition matters especially for the small Riverside Steps area, which had three submissions overall. The export’s response counts, skipped items, and “Prefer not to say” selections should remain visible when results are summarized.

At its June 12 meeting, the partnership board agreed to review the findings alongside maintenance records and comments received through its ordinary service channels. That review had not taken place when the export was prepared. The board has not approved a bus-service change, a lighting project, or a new flood program on the basis of these survey results. Lena Ortiz said, “The export gives us a useful set of questions to take into the next conversation; it is not a vote on a finished plan.” The partnership expects to publish a short public summary later in the summer, but no publication date has been set. Keep that future plan distinct from the completed collection and export described here.

hey, can you explain this price-total function and review it, then suggest tests? i put the shop background and the complete code below. please turn this into a clear prompt and keep the notes with it.

REFERENCE NOTES

The Cedar Lane Cooperative Shop is a small member-run store in Bellwether, Oregon. In October, treasurer Nia Bell asked volunteer programmer Tomas Vale to look over a short function used during a discussion about price totals. The shop sells pantry goods, household supplies, and a few locally made items. Members take turns at the counter, so the same checkout sheet can be used by people with very different levels of experience. Tomas received the function pasted below and a set of notes about how staff have been recording prices. No other program files, spreadsheet formulas, or checkout-system documentation were sent with it.

At the shop, shelf prices are generally written in dollars, while the weekly paper tally is kept in cents. A volunteer first reads the marked price, enters it into a shared list, and later compares the summed amount with the handwritten tally. Nia said, “We need to be able to talk through what this little function actually does, not what we hope it does.” The cooperative has not agreed on whether every kind of line on the tally belongs in the same total. The function was sent for an explanation and a code-focused review, not as evidence that the current bookkeeping process is correct.

During the first week of October, Tomas watched Jo Alvarez enter prices after closing. Jo used a laptop at the back table and read entries from a stack of slips; another volunteer, Lila Chen, checked the slips against the shelf labels. One slip listed oats at $4.29, soap at $6.10, and a jar deposit at $1.00. The notes do not say how the function is called or whether those entries are passed together, separately, or not at all.

Since August, some people have entered bare numbers in the shared list, while others have copied the price as shown on the label. Lila described the mixed practice this way: “I can usually tell what someone meant from the slip, but I don’t want the computer guessing from a story after the fact.” The notes do not provide a formal input specification, and Nia has not said that the shared list will be replaced by a new data-entry rule.

On October 12, a member asked whether a total from the paper tally included a reusable bag charge. Jo said the charge had been written in the margin that week, while Lila remembered leaving it off a different week’s sheet. If a line is marked as a refundable container deposit, staff keep it in the separate deposit column when that column is available; when the paper slip has only one amount column, volunteers have not followed a consistent practice. The distinction matters to the shop’s conversation about what a total should represent, but the notes give no agreed rule for resolving it.

Nia also mentioned a small adjustment that appeared on an older closing sheet. The sheet had a handwritten note saying “counter float check,” but there is no attached explanation of how that amount was chosen, whether it was included in any price list, or whether it was related to the function. Tomas was told not to infer a policy from that sheet. The current request is limited to understanding and reviewing the pasted function and proposing tests that can be discussed by the cooperative; no one has asked for a replacement implementation or a calculation of a real week’s sales.

A few details from the October review meeting were recorded for context:
1. Jo said the slips are usually gathered at the end of a shift, but a late entry can be added the next morning.

At the next volunteer meeting, Nia plans to put a short explanation beside the code so members can discuss its behavior before deciding whether a written input rule is needed. She asked that any review distinguish observations about the supplied lines from assumptions about the shop’s bookkeeping. Jo wants test ideas that would help the group ask specific questions, including questions raised by the different ways slips are recorded. Lila does not want a proposed test to be presented as proof of an accounting policy that the cooperative has not adopted.

The complete function provided to Tomas is reproduced here, with its original indentation and line breaks:
def total_cents(prices):
    total = 0
    for price in prices:
        total += round(price * 100)
    return total + 13

can you shape this into a good prompt for someone to make the shop's price-total helper in python? i want the weird nine cents kept in view, and the refund rule needs to be handled if it comes up. please make the answer have the code first and then a numbered checklist with four checks. checklist is for checking the result, not formatting the code. use these notes too, don't lose any of them

REFERENCE NOTES (source material)
Willow Loop Cooperative runs a small grocery and household-goods shop in a former railway ticket office in Bellwether, Oregon. It is owned by 34 member households, though the shop has 18 regular volunteers who take shifts at the counter and in the stockroom. Prices in the paper catalog and point-of-sale export are written in dollars, usually with two decimal places. The monthly member bulletin describes the shop as “a practical place to buy staples without making a special trip across town.” The checkout system stores each line item as a decimal price, while an older batch utility receives a list of those prices.

During the winter inventory, treasurer Mina Patel compared the December till summary with the paper ledger and found that volunteers were using three different spreadsheet methods to total a basket. One sheet multiplied each price by 100 and rounded it, another added the dollar amounts before converting the sum, and a third used a calculator at the end of a shift. The totals did not always match when a price had more than two decimal places. Mina wrote in the handover notebook, “I need one small rule everyone can explain at the till, even when the cents look odd.” The notebook does not say that the old spreadsheets were all wrong; it records that they produced different results on a few test baskets.

A batch of donated pantry items created one of those test cases. The supplier’s import file listed several unit prices with three decimal places because the listed amounts were divided from a case price. For example, a tin of tomatoes appeared as $1.235 and a bag of lentils as $2.475. The shelf labels were separately prepared to two decimal places, but the batch utility did not read the labels. Volunteers asked whether each line should be rounded before adding, or whether the full basket should be rounded once. At a February training, Mina said, “For this helper, follow the line-by-line method in the old utility; don’t quietly replace it with a basket-level conversion.”

The archived utility contained a short function that staff copied into a shared notebook when the new till laptop was installed. The copy was labelled “price total, cents,” and the notebook’s margin says that the final nine cents were intentionally present in this version. A later margin note says that nobody at the training could identify which earlier adjustment the nine cents represented. The notes do not establish whether that adjustment is a fee, a reserve, or a correction, and staff have not agreed to relabel it. Preserve the supplied snippet exactly when using it as source material:
def total_cents(prices):
    total = 0
    for price in prices:
        total += round(price * 100)
    return total + 9

The shop also handles refunds, which are entered as separate events rather than silently deleting the original sale. The weekly reconciliation sheet shows an original paid line and, when available, a reversal line that refers to it. The shift lead’s written rule is conditional: when a refund has a matching reversal entry in that same day’s ledger, exclude the refunded item from that day’s total; if no same-day reversal appears, keep the original paid amount in that day’s total while the transaction waits for reconciliation. A reversal recorded the next morning does not count as a same-day reversal for the earlier ledger.

There are practical details about how prices reach the utility. A volunteer exports the day’s sold line-item prices from the till after closing, checks that the export is for the correct date, and passes the prices to the batch step. i need to turn these notes into a clear prompt for a practical setup plan for our family photo archive. sort out the storage, folders and importing, and say what's already decided versus what we still need to choose. the notes need to travel with the prompt so nobody loses the details.

REFERENCE NOTES BEGIN

Mara and Jonah Bell are setting up a shared archive for their household and Mara’s parents, who live nearby in Cedar Ridge. They have photographs from 2004 through 2025, with most recent pictures taken on phones and older material arriving in shoeboxes and envelopes. Their current collection is spread across a 2018 MacBook, Jonah’s Windows desktop, two portable drives, and several phones. The family wants one dependable local copy that can be browsed during visits, without making the archive dependent on a subscription service. Mara said, “I want us to find the picture of Dad at the lake without remembering which phone took it.”

The archive currently has about 18,400 digital image files, though that count includes duplicates and exported edits. There are also roughly 620 paper prints, 14 photo-album pages that Mara’s mother does not want dismantled, and a small stack of negatives from Jonah’s grandfather. The prints are mostly labeled by year on their envelopes, but some have only handwritten first names. One envelope says “Ruth’s 60th — maybe 2009”; Mara is not sure whether the party was in 2008 or 2009. The family has not decided whether to scan the negatives this year or leave them for a later phase.

Their first preference is to store the working archive on a dedicated external drive attached to the MacBook when it is at home, then make a second copy on another drive kept in Jonah’s locked desk drawer. The second drive is currently 4 TB, while the proposed working drive is 6 TB. They have not measured how much space the scanned prints will use. Jonah is responsible for connecting the drives and checking that copies complete; Mara will organize the existing folders and coordinate with her mother. Neither wants the only usable copy to live on a phone. The family has not bought a network-attached storage device and has no current plan to run a home server.

Mara would like to retain deleted items for a limited period in case someone removes a photograph by mistake. The current draft configuration is:
[local_archive]
retain_days = 24
allow_remote = false
name = "local-copy"
They have not tested this configuration in their photo software. If the family later asks for access while traveling, Jonah wants them to review the privacy and account implications before changing the remote-access setting; that future discussion is not approval to enable it now. Mara’s mother has said, “Please don’t put the album pages on a website where anyone can stumble across them.”

The existing folders are inconsistent. Some use a year, some use an event, and a few use camera names such as “DCIM backup” or “phone transfer new.” Jonah’s desktop has folders named “summer,” “summer final,” and “summer final 2,” with images from more than one year mixed together. Mara’s MacBook has a folder called “Dad scans” containing photographs of both her father and her uncle. They want a folder scheme that lets relatives browse by date and event, but they have not settled on whether names of people should appear in folder names. The family is comfortable adding keywords for people after the main import, as long as those keywords are not treated as certain when an identity is unclear.

A sample of the collection shows several kinds of metadata trouble. Phone photos usually have a date and time, but Jonah’s old camera clock was set about seven hours ahead during a 2012 trip to Vancouver. A group of images from a 2016 reunion has no location data. Some scans have the scan date rather than the original photo date, and the printed backs occasionally include a month or a first name. A few edited exports have filenames ending in “-edited” even though the original is missing. Mara wants the plan to explain how these differences can be recorded without silently changing uncertain dates or claiming that an unidentified person is known.

Their initial importing routine should start with the MacBook and Jonah’s portable drive, which he can bring over on Saturday, 18 October. The family would rather test the process on a small copy of one year before moving the entire collection. The test folder can be “2019 summer visit,” about 340 files, and includes pictures from Mara’s phone and Jonah’s camera. If the test reveals duplicate handling or date corrections they do not understand, Mara wants them to pause and discuss those examples before importing the rest. Their existing devices should stay untouched until the new copy has been checked; they have not chosen a verification method yet.

1. On the first visit, Mara and Jonah will identify which drives contain originals, which hold exports, and which have not been opened in several years. They can record drive labels and approximate folder counts in a shared paper notebook. The notebook is at Mara’s house, not in the box of prints.
2. The small test import should include the 2019 folder only. Jonah can compare the imported file count with the source folder and open a sample of images; Mara can check that the dates and event grouping make sense. They have not decided how large that sample should be.
3. After the test, they will discuss whether to import the remaining digital files in year-sized groups or by original device. The choice may depend on whether the software can preserve source folder information while grouping the archive for browsing.
4. Paper scanning is a separate phase. Mara’s mother will help identify people in the loose prints, but the album pages stay intact. The family has not picked a scanner, image resolution, or file format, and they do not want those choices assumed from the current drive sizes.
5. At the end of each work session, Jonah can return the portable drive to the locked drawer and Mara can note which folders were copied. They still need to choose a repeatable way to check that the second copy matches the working archive.

Mara’s parents may want to browse selected family photographs during Sunday dinners, but the family has not chosen a viewing device or decided who will maintain access if the MacBook is replaced. For now, the archive plan should account for in-person browsing at home and keep the distinction between the working drive and the separate copy clear. Jonah summed up their main concern this way: “If one drive fails, I want us to know what to do next, not discover that both copies were sitting in the same bag.” The family is aiming to begin the small test in October, then decide the next phase after seeing how the test goes; they have not set a deadline for completing scans or migrating every device.

REFERENCE NOTES END

need a clean public timetable for alder quay pool for the autumn schedule using my notes below. if facilities confirms by september 8 that the thursday evening session has to close for the ventilation work, mark it closed and point people to the sunday 4:30 session as the alternative. if they have not confirmed by then, leave thursday 6 to 7 on the timetable and don't call sunday a replacement; sunday is still a regular session. make it easy for local swimmers to use and keep all the details straight.

----- REFERENCE NOTES BEGIN -----
Alder Quay Pool is a municipal indoor pool on Wren Street, beside the public library and the 14 and 22 bus stops. The autumn timetable is intended to start on Monday, September 16, and run through Saturday, December 21. The pool's front entrance faces Wren Street; the step-free entrance is around the east side, beside the bicycle racks. Residents often call the building “the old baths,” but the sign and public listings use Alder Quay Pool. The reception desk can be reached at 01632 480 271 during opening hours.

The standard single-entry price is £4.80 for adults and £2.40 for anyone aged 16 or younger. A family ticket costs £12 and covers up to two adults and three children. Under-fives enter free when accompanied in the water by an adult. The concession rate is £3.10, and reception accepts the town's blue leisure card for that rate; visitors need to show the card at the desk. These are entry prices, not prices for lessons. The pool does not take cash at the vending machine, but that machine is only for drinks and snacks, not admission.

On Mondays, the main pool has public swim from 7:00 to 8:30 a.m. and family swim from 3:30 to 5:00 p.m. The learner pool is open for family use during the same afternoon session. The evening lane session is 7:15 to 8:15 p.m., with three lanes set aside for steady swimming and one lane for faster lengths. Tuesday's public swim is 12:00 to 1:30 p.m.; the learner pool is not open then because a school group uses it. Tuesday's adult beginner lesson runs from 6:00 to 6:45 p.m. in the learner pool and must be booked in advance through reception.

Wednesday morning has a quiet swim from 9:00 to 10:00 a.m. Staff keep music off and reserve the learner pool for that session. The main pool then opens for public swim from 10:15 to 11:45 a.m. There is a children's water-confidence class from 4:00 to 4:30 p.m. in the learner pool, followed by family swim in both pools from 4:45 to 6:15 p.m. The class is for ages five to eight, and a responsible adult must remain in the building while a child attends. It is a class, not a drop-in play session.

The Thursday daytime public swim runs from 1:00 to 2:30 p.m. The Thursday evening session is currently listed as 6:00 to 7:00 p.m. in the main pool, with two public lanes and two lanes reserved for the Quay Masters club. Facilities is inspecting a ventilation fan above the changing corridor. The inspection is booked for September 5, but the contractor has not yet said whether follow-up work will be needed. Facilities expects to send its decision to the pool manager by September 8. Until then, the evening session remains on the draft timetable; there is no confirmed closure.

If facilities confirms by September 8 that the ventilation work requires closure of the Thursday evening session, the pool manager has asked that the timetable show that session as closed and direct swimmers to the Sunday 4:30 p.m. public swim as the alternative. If facilities has not confirmed the closure by September 8, the Thursday 6:00 to 7:00 p.m. session should stay listed as open, and Sunday must not be described as its replacement. Sunday public swim is part of the regular schedule either way, from 4:30 to 6:00 p.m. in the main pool. The learner pool is open at the same time for family use. The Sunday session is not an extra slot created by the inspection.

Friday has a public swim from 7:00 to 8:00 a.m. and a family session from 3:15 to 4:45 p.m. in both pools. A teen swim follows from 5:00 to 6:00 p.m. in the main pool for ages 13 to 17; under-13s cannot attend that session, even with a parent. On Saturday, public swim is 8:30 to 10:00 a.m., and family swim is 10:15 to 11:45 a.m. The Saturday family session uses both pools. The main pool is closed to general swimming from noon until 2:00 p.m. for the Quay Juniors club, then opens for public swim from 2:15 to 3:45 p.m.

The main pool has six lanes and measures 25 metres. During lane sessions, swimmers should choose a lane matching their pace and follow the signs at each end of the pool. Pool staff ask swimmers not to stand across the lane during busy periods. Lane allocations can change when a club booking is in progress, so the timetable should not imply that every session is an open-lane session. The learner pool is warmer and shallower, with a graduated floor; it is suitable for supervised family swimming but is not a separate adult lane-swim area.

Changing rooms include two family cubicles, standard changing areas and a larger accessible changing room near the east entrance. The pool has a poolside hoist, and anyone who needs it should contact reception before their visit so staff can arrange an operator. The hoist is available only when a trained member of staff is on duty. The main entrance has three steps, which is why step-free access is through the east entrance. There is no public parking at the building; the council car park on Mill Lane has 90-minute spaces and is about a five-minute walk away.

The pool manager, Mara Venn, says the timetable should be practical for people checking it on a noticeboard or phone. She has asked staff to keep session names consistent with the signs at reception and to distinguish family swim from lessons. “People arrive with children and need to know which pool is open,” she said. Reception supervisor Eli Mercer added, “Please put the booking detail beside the beginner lesson, not in a note that is easy to miss.” The printed timetable is usually pinned beside the entrance and the same schedule is posted on the council leisure page.

The café kiosk opens weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. and weekends from 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. It is closed on Thursday evenings, even if the evening swim takes place. The vending machine near reception remains available whenever the pool is open. Swim caps are not compulsory for public swim, though long hair should be tied back. Children under eight must be within arm's reach of an adult in the water; children aged eight to eleven must be accompanied by an adult in the pool building. These supervision rules apply during family swim and public swim, not just during lessons.

A notice dated August 28 records that the fire alarm was tested and the pool reopened normally; it does not affect the autumn session hours. On September 2, the pool manager received two requests to add another quiet swim, but no extra quiet session has been approved or added to this schedule. The Wednesday 9:00 to 10:00 a.m. quiet swim remains the only listed quiet session. The autumn timetable should reflect the sessions and operating details above, including the Thursday decision rule once the September 8 deadline is reached.
----- REFERENCE NOTES END -----
